title: Chapter 23: The SSA-CMM Ladder
text: *Assemble evidence of what you and your systems can do in one stated domain, identify the next missing demonstration, and improve it without treating a chapter, a tool, or a sale as a maturity certificate.*

title: A sale does not tell Maya which level she has reached
text: Maya has a larger collection than the one she began with. It contains source-linked examples, current instructions, verdicts, a recovery practice, delegation and review procedures, system contracts, and a product experiment. The fictional case has also reached one agreed paid pilot and a revised pack accepted for rehearsal. The economics exercise has made the owner's workload visible. She could arrange those records into a persuasive story of progress. She could also attach a high SSA-CMM label to that story and stop asking what the records actually demonstrate. The danger is especially clear after a buyer agrees to pay. Commercial agreement changes the evidence about that particular offer; it does not establish that a memory write survived, a delegated workflow escalates correctly, or a replacement provider preserves behavior. This chapter asks Maya to make a capability portfolio. It is an ordinary evidence table with links, scope, observations, and the next repair. It brings the book's work together without adding another maturity framework. A portfolio is useful when someone can inspect a claim and find the conditions under which it held, including what happened when an important condition changed. The case's examples remain authored fiction and constructed teaching specimens. Their literal inputs and outputs help you learn to judge evidence. They are not receipts of real model runs, customer transactions, or observed learner effects. Your portfolio must contain your own demonstrations when you claim an operational capability. Copying Maya's successful rows would preserve the lesson while inventing your result. Bring the capability-portfolio artifact, your earlier practice records, and one recurring task you understand well enough to review. Begin by asking what claim those records can bear, rather than which title would look best above them.

title: Keep the actual ladder visible
text: The main TFIS homepage names six levels: L0 Task Operator, L1 AI-Assisted Operator, L2 Workflow Orchestrator, L3 Agent Supervisor, L4 Multi-Agent Architect, and L5 Sovereign Architect. Those are the canonical names used in this book. The model expresses TFIS's proposed capability progression; it is not presented here as a validated psychological test or an independently certified professional standard. (The Future Is Solo, n.d.-b) The Functional Life uses different names for four positions: Manual Operator at L0, Tool User at L1, Workflow Builder at L2, and Loop Engineer at L4. L3 and L5 retain the same names. Its treatment particularly emphasizes preserving judgments and verifying their durable use as the loop closes. The difference is disclosed because “Multi-Agent Architect” and “Loop Engineer” direct attention to related but distinct aspects of a system. (The Future Is Solo, n.d.-a) !The six SSA-CMM levels, with higher-level evidence requiring review, durable judgment, and portable operations. The diagram is a navigation aid. Its text alternative is the sequence just given, moving from direct task operation through assistance, workflows, supervision, multi-agent architecture, and sovereignty. The book's evidence checks explain how to investigate those capabilities in practice; they do not turn the illustration into a certification procedure. A level should help you choose the next useful demonstration. If it becomes a way to avoid examining a weak dependency, it has stopped helping. A well-understood manual procedure can be a better current choice than a fragile automated one, even while you develop the ability to delegate more of the work.

title: State the domain before the claim
text: “I can supervise agents” is too broad to inspect. Supervising a bounded draft from synthetic notes differs from supervising a system that can spend money, communicate externally, or change a production database. The task, inputs, permitted actions, review requirements, and consequences determine what the claim needs to establish. Maya chooses a narrow domain for this portfolio: preparing and reviewing action-list examples and the associated workshop-design pack. Her current source-representation instruction remains `instructions-v3`, reached through `learning-loop-v1`. The paid pilot adds delivery and buyer-review evidence within the story. It does not silently broaden that instruction into permission for customer communication or deployment. Write the claim as an operation with conditions. “Given these authorized notes and the current instruction, I can produce a source-linked proposed action list, preserve the specified uncertainty, and identify when clarification is needed” can be challenged. It names the input, useful output, and an important limit. “I am good with AI” leaves all three open. Then identify how much help the performance required. Did you choose each next step? Did an assistant execute a bounded sequence? Did you supply the expected answer? Did another person diagnose the failure? Those forms of support can all be useful, but hiding them makes the portfolio less informative about what you can repeat. You may have strong evidence in one domain and little in another. Keep that unevenness visible. The ability to review a familiar workshop example does not transfer automatically to a medical claim, a legal agreement, or an unfamiliar software system. A portfolio earns its value by locating the boundary of your judgment as well as its strength.

title: L0: make direct work inspectable
text: At L0, begin with the work you perform directly. Select a recurring task, describe its input and useful result, and record what happens when you do it. The objective is to make the task and its cost visible enough that later assistance can be compared with something meaningful. Maya's early baseline asked her to notice where workshop design required research, interpretation, drafting, and review. The most useful observation was not that a document took a certain number of minutes. It was that a credible workshop brief needed an activity producing participant work she could inspect. That understanding gave later outputs a criterion beyond speed or polished wording. Your evidence can be a modest packet: the original input, your unaided attempt, a note about the decisions you made, and the criteria used to review it. When you make a mistake, preserve it with the correction. A baseline consisting only of your best final answer leaves no account of the work a tool might genuinely change. Do not make the baseline artificially difficult to create a dramatic comparison. Use comparable material and the same completion standard when you later evaluate assistance. Include review and repair in both conditions where they are part of completing the task. A faster draft that leaves essential checking for later has not yet demonstrated faster completed work. The next practical move is small: select a recurring part whose desired input and output you can explain, and prepare a saved instruction for assistance. If you cannot say what a good result preserves, returning to direct work and domain learning is an appropriate repair. The baseline helps you find that missing judgment before a tool reproduces the uncertainty at greater speed.

title: L1: demonstrate useful assistance across actual attempts
text: L1 concerns assistance applied to a task you can still judge. A reusable prompt is a starting artifact. Evidence requires actual attempts, the material supplied, the first outputs, and the corrections needed. A prompt that exists but has never been used establishes that you wrote an instruction, not that it produces the intended result. The Functional Life suggests repeated use of a saved task prompt, including a five-run starter exercise. Treat that count as a practical invitation to observe variation, not a scientifically established reliability threshold. A narrow set of easy cases can pass repeatedly while leaving an important failure untouched. (The Future Is Solo, n.d.-a) Maya's early action-list examples show why the first response matters. An output can copy a plausible owner into an unassigned task or turn “soon” into a date. If she saves only the repaired answer, she loses the distinction between what the assistant initially did and what her intervention made correct. For your demonstration, choose related inputs that vary a consequential feature. Include an explicit date in one, imprecise timing in another, and a suggestion that resembles a commitment. Keep expected answers separate during drafting. Review the fields against their own source passages, record the help required, and explain the error before asking for another answer. The next repair follows the evidence. An ambiguous instruction may need clearer wording. A correct supplied rule that was violated may require better source extraction, checking, or a different choice of assistance. An unfamiliar subject may require learning or expert review. Adding instructions indiscriminately does not distinguish these problems and can leave you with a long prompt whose effective behavior remains unclear.

title: L2: connect steps without losing their contracts
text: L2 moves the unit of work from a single assisted task to a repeatable workflow. The useful evidence concerns the connections: what one step receives, what it returns, what the next step may assume, and what happens when a prerequisite is missing or a check fails. Maya's workflow separates source extraction, drafting, comparison against the original material, bounded repair, and a human evidence packet. Its steps exist because they answer different questions. Extraction identifies what the source establishes. Drafting proposes a useful representation. Review compares that proposal with its support. A second polished draft is not a substitute for the independent comparison the workflow requires. To demonstrate the chain, retain one complete run from input through reviewed result. Record the actual handoffs, not just an arrow diagram. Then introduce a safe missing dependency in a rehearsal copy. The workflow should identify the absent input or stale version and hold the step that depends on it. A chain that continues by inventing missing material is operating, but it is not satisfying its contract. This level can include substantial human direction. If you manually supply every stage, say so. You are testing a repeatable procedure and its interfaces. That practice can prepare delegation without pretending that the whole sequence already runs independently. The next move is to define a bounded unit another executor can carry through without asking you to choose every internal step. Preserve the inputs, return contract, allowed decisions, and escalation conditions. If the chain cannot explain what to do when a source is unavailable, making it more autonomous will not supply the missing policy.

title: L3: show that supervision changes the result when it should
text: At L3, the evidence must reach beyond a delegation document. A bounded agent or executor should perform the authorized sequence, return a reviewable result, and bring the right unresolved conditions to the human. The supervisor must then inspect the consequential meaning rather than merely approve the presence of an output. Chapter 17's contract makes the distinction concrete. It allows a proposed candidate and a limited repair, with a hold when a material defect persists. It does not authorize external communication, source edits, or changes to authoritative memory. A real demonstration would record the executor's actual actions and returns under those limits, including how the human responded. Chapter 18 adds a supervision failure: an initially accepted concise draft merges distinct objects and conceals a conflict. The repaired review withdraws that acceptance and checks the particular version against the source. A portfolio should preserve such an event because it shows what supervision needs to catch. Deleting the first judgment would make the procedure appear more dependable than its history supports. For your own run, include a condition that should be escalated and a covered uncertainty that should remain in a useful partial answer. A missing authorized source can hold drafting. An unassigned owner already covered by the instruction should remain visible without halting every other part. The distinction tests whether the contract guides decisions, rather than turning “ask the human” into a universal escape from the task. The supervisor's workload belongs in the evidence. Record the review needed to catch defects and the tasks kept pending when capacity was exhausted. If supervising the current operation costs more effort than performing it directly, that is information about the present design. You may narrow the delegation while improving it, without pretending that unrestricted autonomy is the required next step.

title: L4: inspect coordination and the retained judgment
text: The canonical L4 name directs attention to architecture across agents. The Functional Life's Loop Engineer name directs attention to feedback that persists and is used. For the book's practical portfolio, describe both the actual architecture you operate and what happens to the human judgments that should improve its later work. Do not replace either description with an agent count. Chapter 19's separate drafting and checking roles illustrate an architectural responsibility: their outputs must refer to the same source packet and candidate version before they can be joined. Two draft returns do not supply an independent check. A report that examined the old candidate cannot approve the revised one. These relationships make coordination inspectable and give a failed join a specific repair. The verdict practice adds a second requirement. A useful correction identifies its target, reason, scope, and current status. An actual completed write must be reopened. A later attempt must receive the applicable verdict and apply its meaning to changed input. Copying the old answer is not the same operation as using the retained judgment. V13-01 gives you a precise challenge: avoid inventing a date when the source says “soon,” while retaining a date that a new input explicitly supplies. A later run that changes every date to “unknown” has overgeneralized the correction. Keep the input, retrieved verdict, actual response, and review together so the failure can be traced to retrieval, interpretation, application, or authority. The book's manual ledger and constructed role packets make these operations understandable. They do not supply evidence that your agents performed them. If your current arrangement is one assistant with manual handoffs, describe it accurately and choose the next warranted demonstration. Additional agents are useful only when their distinct responsibilities and coordination improve a defined operation enough to justify the extra work.

title: L5: preserve the operation when a dependency changes
text: At L5, the question extends beyond producing a correct answer in a familiar environment. Can the necessary records, judgment history, permissions, and operating procedures survive a meaningful change of provider, tool, location, or responsible person? Can you restore a usable state and identify what still depends on someone else's infrastructure? The portability drill provides a starting distinction. An exact copy may preserve a stale instruction. A readable file may have lost the annotation that explained its scope. A new model may receive the correct packet and still mishandle a conflict. Each condition needs its own observation and repair. Choose a dependency your actual workflow has, and rehearse its loss without damaging active work. Rebuild the selected operation from the portable package, inspect current authority, perform a changed-input task, and recover from a deliberately missing source. Where provider substitution matters, record an actual second-provider attempt under known conditions. Opening files in another editor is useful evidence about access; label the model behavior untested if no model comparison occurred. Document how someone else could continue the necessary work within its authority, including where that person must seek expertise or permission. The goal is understandable continuity, not pretending that every judgment has been removed from the human role. A procedure can remain dependent on a specialist while making that dependency explicit and planning around it. Economic sustainability also matters to the larger solo-enterprise claim. A portable system that consumes more owner attention and cost than its activity can support has not solved that business problem. Chapter 22's model and the pilot's actual scope therefore belong beside technical evidence, with their assumptions intact. Revenue, margin, and level are different judgments; none should be used as a shortcut around the others.

title: Use the five pillars to find a missing question
text: The main TFIS account names Agency, Clarity, Competence, Accountability, and Security as five pillars. Use those names to inspect the selected operation from different directions, not to create a new weighted average. The source's self-assessment can prompt reflection, but this portfolio requires the relevant observable work. (The Future Is Solo, n.d.-b) For Maya, Agency asks which part can proceed under the agreed limits and where her presence remains necessary. Clarity asks whether the buyer's task, deliverable, exclusions, and acceptance criteria are actually understood. Competence asks whether she can explain a source error or recover the procedure without relying on fluent reassurance. Accountability asks where the review decision is recorded and how she knows the completed state matches it. Security asks what material and actions are permitted, which dependencies are retained, and whether a move preserves the necessary boundaries. These questions should lead you to particular records and demonstrations. Do not average a critical missing condition into a reassuring score. Strong drafting ability does not cancel unknown permission to use the source. A readable archive does not compensate for an obsolete current selector. Mark the specific dependency unresolved and hold the operation that relies on it. You can continue other authorized work while repairing that gap.

title: Work through an overstated portfolio entry
text: Maya's first candidate entry says, “L4 complete: verdict ledger implemented and next-run improvement verified.” The attached evidence is the book's V13-01 packet: an authored bad answer, a reviewed correction, a changed input, and expected properties. It makes the distinction understandable, but contains no receipt of an actual agent write or later run. She repairs the entry rather than discarding the useful packet. The claim becomes: “I can explain and rehearse scoped verdict review using this specimen; actual durable write and changed-input use in my configured workflow remain to be demonstrated.” The source links stay. The unsupported completion statement is removed. The next action now has a visible purpose. A second entry initially says, “Provider independence passed,” pointing to a copied Markdown package. The supplied record establishes that files can be opened and their relationships inspected in another location. Without an actual second-provider attempt, the claim must remain narrower. Maya labels file portability separately and leaves provider behavior untested. These repairs make the next demonstration concrete enough to perform. For the verdict case, save an approved record in the authorized location, reopen it, supply it through the maintained route, and keep the actual changed-input output. For provider behavior, choose a permitted receiving environment and inspect what it does with the same task and material. The worked portfolio supplies these entries and routes to the existing artifacts. It distinguishes a demonstration resource from a reader's execution evidence. You can use that distinction throughout the book: a template helps you produce a record; it does not supply the observation that should fill it.

title: Choose one gap that blocks the next useful operation
text: Before selecting that gap, give a reviewer a route through one existing claim. Begin with the operation being claimed, then let the reviewer find the actual input, instruction version, output, and judgment. Allow them to ask which detail supports the judgment. If you have to fill the crucial connection from memory, add it to the record after checking it. For a concrete rehearsal, use Chapter 7's run-02 and the current instruction route. Run-02 is a constructed specimen associated with v2; the route now selects v3 after Chapter 11. A careless portfolio entry might call it a successful test of the current instruction because its link still opens. The historical claim is narrower: it illustrates the earlier handling of “soon” under the displayed v2 instruction. The reviewer should preserve that useful history and ask for a fresh observation before claiming current execution behavior. This is the same distinction that matters when software, prompts, source packets, permissions, or model settings change. Have the reviewer inspect a rejected result too. They should be able to identify the defect, why the repair addresses it, and what the repaired result still leaves unresolved. This prevents a portfolio from becoming a gallery of polished answers with no evidence of how consequential errors are recognized. You do not need to expose an entire private archive for this review. Prepare the smallest authorized packet that permits the claim to be checked, preserving source meaning and status. If confidentiality prevents a material part from being shared, state the limitation and arrange an appropriate review method. Removing the evidence and retaining the confidence would change what an outside reader can assess. A portfolio can become an excuse to collect more proof than the work needs. Avoid trying to complete every possible challenge before performing a modest authorized task. Identify the operation you want to rely on next, then find the missing condition that would make reliance unjustified. If the next step is another draft-only pilot pack, you may need a dependable source review and a realistic delivery window more urgently than a multi-provider architecture. If the next step is unattended overnight processing, missing escalation and recovery evidence becomes much more consequential. The appropriate demonstration follows the intended use, not the prestige of a level. Write the repair as an observable event. “Improve memory” is vague. “A changed-input attempt retrieves V13-01 through the current route, preserves a newly explicit date, and leaves a reviewable record” states what you will inspect. Define the failure result too: if it copies the old answer or reads a superseded instruction, locate that dependency before expanding the task. Then repeat the relevant check under the repaired conditions. If your change affects earlier behavior, include the earlier case. If it changes only a broken link, verify the route and dependent operation rather than rerunning every unrelated exercise. The portfolio should help you select meaningful work and stop redundant checking when the claim has the evidence it needs.

title: Revisit a claim when its conditions change
text: A capability portfolio describes a working state, so maintenance should follow changes to that state. An instruction revision, different model, broader permission, new source format, or revised deliverable can invalidate part of an earlier demonstration without making every other observation worthless. Record which conditions the claim depended on so that you can identify the affected evidence. Suppose your workflow previously accepted pasted text, but the next task introduces photographed notes. The source-faithfulness rule may remain sensible. The extraction operation now has an additional dependency: the handwriting must be read accurately before the action list can be judged. Keep the old text-input evidence and add the new transcription-and-source comparison required by the changed task. Or suppose a draft-only assistant is given permission to save a candidate file. The existing semantic checks do not establish that the write reaches the intended folder or leaves the source unchanged. Add a bounded write-and-reopen demonstration and inspect the permission setting. If the tool cannot safely express the intended write scope, keep the save manual while the rest of the useful workflow continues. Use plain status words for portfolio claims: current under the stated conditions, historical, awaiting a relevant check, or withdrawn after a discovered problem. These describe evidence applicability rather than your identity. A withdrawn claim can remain valuable history when its reason helps prevent someone from relying on it again. Maya's earlier withdrawal of a mistaken acceptance offers the same lesson at a smaller scale. The correction should be visible at the point of reliance, not hidden in an unrelated note. When an operating claim changes, update the portfolio and the procedure that depends on it. Leave unrelated evidence alone, and record the specific demonstration that would justify renewed reliance.

title: Keep capability and commercial judgment in contact
text: The pilot has made the final distinction unavoidable. Maya may produce a sound pack and still need to change its price, scope, acquisition method, or support. She may have buyer interest in a task that her current procedure cannot safely deliver. A capability portfolio and a product experiment answer different questions, but decisions improve when each can refer to the other. For a service professional, useful evidence could join an agreed scope, a reviewed delivery, actual correction history, and the effort needed to support it. For an educator, it could connect the designed activity, authorized participant work, and the limits of what the review establishes. For a software builder, it could connect a bounded requirement, actual behavior, permission controls, and a tested recovery path. These adaptations do not make expertise interchangeable. They show how the same habit of evidence can travel: name the operation, retain its support, inspect the result, and mark what you cannot yet claim. An advanced label should never authorize you to stop learning the domain whose work you supervise.

title: Field assignment: defend one claim and repair another
text: Complete the capability portfolio for one recurring domain. Link the baseline, actual assisted attempts, workflow, supervision, verdict, recovery, and commercial evidence that are relevant. Mark absent or simulated evidence plainly. Do not manufacture a filled row merely to make the ladder look complete. Select one claim another person could verify from the records, and one that currently overstates them. Explain the first without AI: identify the input, help used, current instruction, output, review, and limit. Rewrite the second so it names the missing demonstration rather than hiding it behind a general confidence statement. Perform that next demonstration where it is authorized and useful. Save the actual first result, including failure. Make a bounded repair, repeat the affected check, and update the portfolio's statement of scope. Your completion evidence is an inspectable claim and a repaired gap, not a numerical average or a self-awarded title. Maya ends with a clearer account of her capabilities and dependencies. The paid pilot remains one fictional commercial event; advanced operational claims still require their particular evidence. Chapter 24 returns to the economic destination and asks what a million-dollar solo company would actually have to sustain.

title: Chapter 24: The Million-Dollar Solo Company
text: *Turn a large economic ambition into explicit assumptions, a workable operating design, and a ninety-day sequence of evidence-producing decisions while preserving human judgment and the freedom to change direction.*

title: A direction large enough to expose the assumptions
text: Maya's first paid pilot has not produced a million-dollar company. In the fictional case, one educator agreed to an illustrative USD 300 engagement and accepted a repaired pack for rehearsal. The pack's initial agenda exceeded the agreed thirty minutes; the repair preserved the participant attempt and revision while reducing the total. There is still no observed learner outcome or payment receipt. That is a more useful place to end this book than an invented leap from one purchase to extraordinary wealth. Maya now has something specific to examine: a buyer situation, a deliverable, a correction, a record of the work involved, and an economic model whose assumptions she can challenge. The remaining distance is visible. The million-dollar question gives that distance a scale. What would have to be true for one person to direct an operation earning a million dollars in annual revenue? Which constraints could change through better design? Which require demand, expertise, cooperation, or capital that has not been established? Which costs would a flattering answer leave out? The Future Is Solo proposes that individual judgment, supported by systems, can direct work at a scale previously associated with larger organizations. We have treated that as a thesis to investigate through practice. Neither its ambition nor the machinery built around it establishes the viability of a particular enterprise. (The Future Is Solo, n.d.-b) Your final artifact is a solo-enterprise plan. It connects a chosen economic direction with the evidence, operating limits, and next decisions needed to pursue it. The plan can lead to a smaller profitable service, an educational product, software, collaboration, or a decision to stop. It should make those choices more informed.

title: Name the million before calculating it
text: “A million-dollar company” can refer to several different things. This chapter's main scenario uses USD 1 million in gross annual revenue: sales earned over a year before business expenses are deducted. That is the target being divided by a unit price. It is not a statement about the owner's bank balance. Profit requires attention to the costs included in the calculation. Chapter 22's economics model separates a cash remainder before owner compensation and tax from an economic contribution that also values owner time. Both can be useful, provided their labels remain attached. A business can appear attractive when the owner works without an allowance and unattractive once that effort is included. Owner income is what the owner receives under the business's actual arrangements. It is constrained by costs, obligations, retained cash, and other claims on the operation. Revenue arriving in the business does not make the same amount available for personal use. An agreed fee is also different from an amount collected, as the pilot record already shows. Valuation is a judgment about what ownership of the business is worth. It is not the annual sales figure renamed. A valuation claim would require its own assumptions and basis; this book does not supply a market multiple that turns Maya's pilot into a priced company. Nor does a hypothetical valuation pay the expenses of the next delivery. Choose the meaning relevant to your purpose, state the currency and period, and keep the others separate. If you want a sustainable owner income, a gross-revenue target alone is an incomplete guide. If you want to build an asset that can continue through a change of operator, its transferable procedures and dependencies matter alongside its sales.

title: Start with the economics that the pilot actually suggests
text: The illustrative baseline allocates four hours to delivery, including repair, two hours to acquisition across the three discovery conversations and two proposals, and one hour to support. The total is seven owner hours for the USD 300 agreed pilot fee. Cash cost is USD 20. Using USD 50 per hour as an assumed value of owner time gives USD 350 of time cost. If the model treats the USD 300 as earned revenue, the unit's economic contribution is negative USD 70: 300 minus 20 minus 350. It tells Maya that the offer needs investigation before she relies on repeated identical sales to support her work. The monthly baseline makes the operating burden clearer. Assume 160 owner hours are available, with forty reserved for fixed operating work. That leaves 120 for units. At seven hours each, seventeen whole units fit, using 119 unit hours and 159 hours overall. Selling and earning all seventeen would produce USD 5,100 in revenue. After USD 340 of unit cash costs and USD 200 of fixed monthly cash costs, the remainder before owner compensation and tax is USD 4,560. Valuing all 159 owner hours at USD 50 creates a USD 7,950 owner-time allowance. The resulting economic contribution is negative USD 3,390. The filled calendar has amplified the baseline problem. As in Chapter 22, these monthly cash remainders assume all modeled revenue is collected and the listed cash costs are paid in the same period; no collection is observed in the pilot. No part of that calculation establishes that seventeen buyers exist or that their work fits the same time allowance. It shows what the stated assumptions imply. The next useful question is which assumption Maya can responsibly change and test, rather than how to make the projection's final cell look more encouraging.

title: Inspect the proposed improvement as a proposal
text: Chapter 22 considers an alternative at USD 750 per unit, USD 35 of unit cash cost, and six owner hours: three for delivery, two for acquisition, and one for support. The same 120 hours available for unit work would allow twenty units, using all 160 owner hours once fixed operating work is included. If all twenty units sold and their revenue were earned under those assumptions, monthly revenue would be USD 15,000. Subtracting USD 700 of unit cash costs and USD 200 of fixed cash costs leaves USD 14,100 before owner compensation and tax. A USD 8,000 allowance for 160 owner hours leaves USD 6,100 of economic contribution in the model. This is a different commercial proposition with unverified requirements. The price must be acceptable to relevant buyers. The three-hour delivery allowance must still produce the agreed result. Acquisition and support must remain within the stated amounts when the actual mix of buyers and problems appears. The useful improvement is that the model now tells Maya what to investigate. She can examine which part of delivery might be narrowed or reused, how a buyer would understand the revised scope, and what could increase support. A failed test then identifies an assumption to change rather than leaving “the business model” as one mysterious object. Keep the baseline beside the proposal. If a later experiment supports one changed assumption but not another, record that uneven result. A buyer might accept the higher fee while delivery still takes four hours. A redesigned pack might be faster to produce while too few people want it. Those outcomes imply different next moves.

title: Follow the arithmetic to the actual capacity gap
text: Twenty units per month at USD 750, repeated across twelve identical fully sold months, annualizes to USD 180,000. That is a conditional calculation. It assumes the same price, completed sales, work requirement, and available capacity throughout the year. It is not a forecast, a pipeline, or revenue the case has achieved. At the same USD 750 price, gross annual revenue of at least USD 1 million would require 1,334 whole units. Those units would produce USD 1,000,500. The proposed capacity is only 240 units across twelve months. The gap remains even if every available slot sells. Under the unchanged six-hour unit assumption, 1,334 units would require 8,004 owner hours for unit work alone, before fixed operations. That is incompatible with the model's 160-hour monthly allocation. More enthusiastic marketing cannot fit those hours into the same operating design. More drafting agents cannot make the customer-facing judgment and support disappear by definition. A different design might change the relationship between a sale and owner work. A reusable resource may require less direct delivery for each buyer. A group format may serve several participants in one supported session. A higher-value service may support a different price. Software may automate a stable operation. Each possibility changes the proposition and introduces its own assumptions. The arithmetic should therefore end one line of reasoning: Maya cannot reach the chosen annual target merely by repeating the proposed pilot unit within the current time budget. It begins another: which useful product and operating arrangement could alter that constraint while preserving quality, demand, and a life she wants to lead?

title: Leave room before promising the modeled ceiling
text: The proposed twenty-unit month uses all 120 hours allocated to units and all forty hours assigned to fixed operations. The model contains no additional owner-time reserve beyond those categories. If a delivery overruns, support increases, or an interruption removes available hours, the same monthly promise no longer fits without something else changing. Maya can choose to commit below the calculated maximum while learning how much variation the work contains. The enterprise plan should name that operating choice and show its effect on revenue and compensation. A reserve is a use of capacity, so it must remain visible rather than being counted simultaneously as free time and sold work. Cash has a related timing problem. A fee can be agreed before cash arrives, while some costs are paid earlier. The pilot supplies no collection record, so the model cannot establish the money available to fund another engagement. For actual work, retain the payment status and the timing of known obligations beside the revenue calculation. A profitable-looking period can still contain a point at which the planned payment is not available. Choose what you are willing to commit before adding the next task. This can include owner hours, cash, the number of simultaneous engagements, and the kinds of promise the current evidence supports. Revisit these limits when actual work shows that the assumptions are too narrow or unnecessarily restrictive. The same discipline applies to continuity. If a service depends on your review, decide what happens when you cannot provide it. A waiting state, an agreed later date, or a qualified collaborator may be more credible than an automatic substitution that has never been tested. Describe that dependency before selling an expectation the operation cannot meet. The ninety-day exercise can reveal the appropriate margin for your situation. Keep the expected work, actual work, and changes in availability separate, then inspect what forced a reschedule or repair. You are learning how the enterprise behaves under ordinary variation. A plan that works only when every unit and every week match the neatest example should remain an experiment rather than a dependable commitment.

title: Decide which constraint deserves the next experiment
text: Capacity is only one possible constraint. An operation may have unused delivery time because few relevant buyers know about it. It may attract interest but lose buyers when the scope is explained. It may sell well and require so much repair that every extra engagement consumes the reserve. Treat those conditions differently. For Maya, the evidence is still too small to name a permanent bottleneck. One fictional pilot exposes a duration-review defect and a demanding unit model. It does not establish a reliable acquisition process, a market-wide price ceiling, or a stable delivery time. Her next experiment should narrow one of those uncertainties. Write the assumption in language that can be checked. “Distribution will improve” is vague. “This specific type of educator has a current brief, recognizes the defined problem, and is willing to consider the stated offer through this permitted contact route” identifies something to investigate. A recipient count alone would not establish the rest. Likewise, “AI will reduce delivery work” should become a particular proposed change. Perhaps a reusable source-linked example removes repeated formatting. Perhaps the review still needs the same attention because each brief has different learning constraints. Record what changes and compare the whole delivery, including correction, before counting a saving. Choose the constraint that blocks the next useful commitment. If you cannot reliably deliver the existing scope, taking on more work is premature. If the delivery is sound but demand remains unknown, another infrastructure project may avoid the relevant question. The enterprise plan should make that trade-off explicit.

title: A service can grow by narrowing and deepening
text: A service route keeps human judgment close to the buyer's particular situation. Maya might learn to distinguish a quick brief review from a deeper activity redesign, with different inputs and delivery boundaries. That could make the work easier to explain and estimate. It would need buyer and delivery evidence before becoming a dependable offer. Higher prices would require a credible useful difference for the chosen buyer. A shorter turnaround, clearer decision, or work supporting a more consequential event might matter in a particular context. Those are hypotheses, not permissions to rename the same uncertain service “premium” and treat the price increase as earned. Standardization can remove repeated work when the repeated part is truly shared. A reusable review sheet, intake format, or source-reference convention may help while leaving the actual design judgment specific to the brief. The cost model must retain whatever review and support remain. A template is valuable when it performs useful work, not when it hides the work someone still has to do. The service route can also lead to a deliberately smaller enterprise. A manageable number of well-scoped engagements, adequate compensation, and protected time may serve the owner's purposes better than the largest available revenue target. Choosing that arrangement after inspecting the evidence is an exercise of agency.

title: An educational product changes the delivery question
text: An educational resource could let an educator use the accumulated examples, criteria, and facilitation guidance without commissioning a full redesign. A group program could combine reusable material with bounded human feedback. Both forms alter how many people may benefit from one piece of preparation, while creating questions about use, support, and continued quality. The next test should examine the part that direct service previously supplied. Can the intended user locate the appropriate activity, understand the criteria, and adapt the material within its stated scope? Where do they need an explanation that is still trapped in Maya's head? An attractive download does not answer those questions. Separate the purchaser from the learner when their roles differ. An educator may buy a facilitator pack, while participants later perform the exercise. Purchase, educator satisfaction, successful facilitation, and learner performance are different evidence. Decide which claim the next test is meant to support and retain the appropriate authorized observation. Do not assume that a digital format removes marginal work. Questions, corrections, accessibility needs, updates, and delivery arrangements can still consume attention or cash. A reusable product changes the pattern of work; its economics need to show where that work went. Test a small version whose dependencies you can inspect before promising support at a scale you have never handled.

title: Software changes what must be maintained
text: A software route becomes interesting when a valuable operation has sufficiently clear inputs, behavior, and review requirements. The action-list practice offers a narrow starting point, but a tool serving real users would need more than a successful synthetic table. Its source handling, permission boundaries, output presentation, error reporting, and recovery would become part of the product. Begin by showing how the proposed interaction helps someone complete a task. A manually delivered prototype can test parts of that experience if it is honestly described. Later, automate the stable operation and inspect the behavior it actually produces. A working interface can still hide a process that requires extensive human rescue. Software can introduce costs that a delivery-only model omits: ongoing maintenance, hosting, monitoring, user support, and handling failures. Put the costs and owner time relevant to your actual design into the model, and mark estimates separately from observed bills and work. The choice of more agents should follow the operation. Distinct roles may help divide evidence gathering, drafting, and checking. They also require correct joins, bounded authority, and review of the resulting state. An additional agent is not an additional buyer, and parallel generation is not evidence that the end-to-end service needs less supervision.

title: Read the real experiments without inventing their ending
text: The TFIS build deck provides a useful counterpart to Maya's constructed case. Its Kosong entry describes a command-line experiment connected to SovMem, open-source distribution, and GitHub Actions runners. Monetization appears as the next question. That distinction is useful: distributing a tool and discovering a sustainable exchange are separate pieces of work. (The Future Is Solo, 2026, slide 39) The AI Fluency go-live entry names work on asset access, delivery, payment-related integration, and email access, then places distribution next. (The Future Is Solo, 2026, slide 40) Another entry describes an AI Ethics in Education course MVP and lists conversion to a paid online course as further work. (The Future Is Solo, 2026, slide 44) These are reported development notes, not independent proof of sales, completed monetization, or learner effectiveness. The pattern matters more than a triumphant ending added by a narrator. A build creates a new possibility and exposes another question. Distribution does not follow automatically from deployment; buying does not follow automatically from attention; educational value does not follow automatically from a payment integration. The next experiment has to address the particular missing relationship. Your records can preserve the same discipline. Write what was built, which behavior was inspected, what a user actually did, and what remains next. Do not move a task from the last category to the first merely because the story would read more smoothly with everything completed.

title: Use the first thirty days to establish a trustworthy baseline
text: The ninety-day plan begins from the present evidence, not from a promised revenue curve. In the first month, choose one offer and a small working scope. Review the pilot record, identify the recurring delivery steps, and keep the acquisition and support work visible. Check whether the assumed cost categories describe the work you would actually have to perform. For Maya, the existing seven-hour pilot record is illustrative. A real reader should replace those values with their own observations from authorized work or a clearly labeled rehearsal. Record interruptions and repair, not only the time the assistant generates text. Distinguish work done once to prepare the service from work expected with each buyer, and keep uncertain classifications open for review. Use discovery to examine the current buyer situation. Obtain appropriate agreement to discuss the work and retain notes. Inspect a relevant brief where permitted. Preserve differences among accounts instead of translating every response into support for the same offer. Keep the number of outreach or proposal attempts bounded by the review and delivery capacity you can actually provide. By the end of the first month, the useful output is a revised experiment record and a source-based cost model. Continue only with an offer whose input, output, acceptance, scope, and effort can be explained. If those remain unclear, narrow the task or return to the relevant capability practice. More commitments would obscure the gap rather than repair it.

title: Use the middle thirty days to test a specific redesign
text: The second month investigates one proposed change to the operating design. Maya's candidate might be a narrower pack whose reusable material reduces repeated delivery work. A different reader might test a group format, a resource used without live explanation, or a more valuable service scope. State the expected useful change and the observation that would challenge it. The USD 750 proposal is available as a modeling scenario, not a price already validated by the case. If you test a different scope and price, describe them clearly to the buyer and record the actual response. A willingness to discuss it remains different from an agreement. A refusal can reveal timing, fit, or value concerns without establishing one universal reason for every buyer. Inspect delivery under the revised arrangement. Keep the first candidate, review, repair, and total work. If the proposal assumes three delivery hours but actual work needs five, preserve five. If reducing the work also removes an essential participant attempt or source review, the apparent efficiency has changed the product's quality standard. At the end of this period, compare the supported assumptions with the original model. Continue, revise, or stop the particular redesign. Do not silently change the target halfway through and then report that the original prediction succeeded. The record should show what changed your decision, including when the answer is that a smaller improvement is all the evidence supports.

title: Use the final thirty days to decide what deserves repetition
text: The third month asks whether the useful parts can be repeated and recovered under the conditions you intend to rely on. Review comparable deliveries or rehearsals, including the failures and support they required. A single unusually easy engagement should not define the operating allowance for a more varied service. Check the dependencies that expansion would make consequential. Can the current procedure be reconstructed from the maintained records? Does a missing source create the right hold? Can you identify the reviewed candidate and distinguish it from a stale one? If another provider or collaborator will be relied on, perform the relevant authorized handoff rather than assuming equivalence. Use the evidence to choose the next commitment. You might repeat a narrowly supported offer, revise price or scope, keep delivery manual, add a specific collaborator, or stop an unpromising route. A plan that allows only expansion cannot respond honestly to what the experiment discovers. The final document should state the offer you will continue, the capacity you can defend, the costs still estimated, the cash and time you will not commit beyond their limits, and the next condition requiring review. The ninety days do not need to end with a million-dollar forecast. They should end with a more dependable basis for your next decision.

title: Decide what solo should mean in your enterprise
text: Solo can describe who owns and directs the operation without implying that the person has no relationships, outside services, or expert help. Your plan should state what you mean by the term. If the target requires contractors, partners, or employees, include their work, cost, authority, and coordination rather than leaving them invisible to preserve the label. Choosing a team can be a sensible response to the work. A task may need expertise you should not improvise, human availability you cannot provide, or collaboration that improves the product. The TFIS thesis can prompt a serious investigation of what one person can direct; it need not become an obligation to reject help that serves the actual purpose. Equally, keeping a smaller operation can be a deliberate design choice. You may prefer a bounded service, a modest product, and enough time to learn and maintain it well. The capability to build larger systems remains useful even when you choose not to maximize their throughput. Make owner attention part of the plan. Name what deserves your judgment, what can proceed under established rules, and what must stop when you are unavailable. A business that uses every free hour to keep its machinery functioning has consumed a resource that the revenue target alone cannot describe.

title: Keep curiosity available after the calendar fills
text: The Functional Life includes exploratory play among its operating practices. Applied to this enterprise, that means retaining some room to investigate questions that are not simply the next delivery task. Such time needs a place in the operating design; it will not reliably appear because an automation was supposed to save it. (The Future Is Solo, n.d.-a) Curiosity also remains useful when it questions the business you have already built. A recurring support problem may reveal a misunderstood user need. A tool failure may show that a dependency should remain manual. A buyer's refusal may reveal an assumption that polished product language had concealed. Protect the ability to hear those signals without defending every earlier choice. TFIS's article *The Meaning of Life: A Techno-Optimist's Response* presents meaning as something developed through building, failure, and learning. Its visible attribution describes an article in Khalil Nooh's voice. We can engage with that stated philosophy without turning its ambitious business question into an achieved result or inventing autobiography on the author's behalf. (The Future Is Solo, n.d.-c) You can take a practical question from it: is the work worth the time and attention you are giving it? Revenue is relevant to that answer because an enterprise must support its obligations. It is not the only measure of whether the activity is useful, understood, or chosen with care.

title: Leave with a plan you can challenge
text: Complete the solo-enterprise plan. Name the economic target precisely, copy the current evidence rather than the hoped-for ending, and show the assumptions that connect price, demand, capacity, cost, and owner work. Choose one operating route and the next experiment it requires. Keep alternatives available where the evidence has not settled the choice. Write the stop and change conditions before the next commitment. If actual delivery exceeds the available window, stop adding work and repair the scope or capacity plan. If source review cannot support the promised output, hold the affected delivery. If buyers do not choose the specific offer, return to the relevant problem or proposition instead of reporting interest as sales. Explain the plan without AI. Show why a million in annual sales is different from owner income or valuation. Show where the proposed twenty-unit month gets its demand and time assumptions. Name the evidence you would need before depending on them. A plan that you cannot explain should not acquire authority because an assistant has formatted it convincingly. Mind gave you a way to ask a useful question, investigate it, and explain what you understand. Memory made the supporting evidence, decisions, and corrections recoverable. System turned those materials into operations you could inspect, delegate within limits, and test against an exchange with someone else. The arcs meet in your ability to create value while knowing what the result does and does not establish. Maya's next step remains a bounded experiment. Yours can be equally concrete: one useful task, one claim to test, one piece of work someone can inspect, and one decision changed by what you learn. The company may grow. The offer may change. What accumulates is the capability to make those choices with understanding, and to build something worth continuing.

title: Practice index: carry one project through the book
text: The chapter artifacts form a working record for one project. You do not need to recreate a document when an existing one already serves the purpose. Link the relevant section, preserve its current version, and add the new evidence where another reader can find it. The tables below identify the work each chapter adds and what to bring forward. They are a navigation aid for the book's exercises, not an additional maturity model or a scored assessment. The canonical SSA-CMM labels and the scope of your evidence are examined in Chapter 23.

title: Mind: establish a question worth pursuing
text: Chapter Working document Carry forward 1 Capability baseline A bounded task, first candidates, criteria, corrections, and remaining gaps. 2 Claim–evidence ledger Claims with source support, limitations, and unresolved hypotheses. 3 Curiosity map A consequential question connected to an observable next inquiry. 4 Inquiry brief Input, proposed learner performance, practice, and a way to judge it. 5 Concept deconstruction Assumptions, explanatory gaps, and reasons behind a useful correction. 6 Connection map A tested comparison across domains and where the analogy breaks. 7 Learning loop An inspectable failed attempt, repair, current selector, and next question. Do not tidy these records by deleting the failed candidate. A later reader needs to see what changed and why. Distinguish an actual attempt in your project from the book's authored practice specimens.

title: Memory: make useful judgment available again
text: Chapter Working document Carry forward 8 Memory inventory What exists, where it is, what is missing, and how it is used. 9 Memory charter Purpose, authority, access, retention, and current-state rules. 10 Memory lanes Separate working context, project state, reusable knowledge, and history. 11 Distillation record Evidence for a reviewed rule change and its verified current destination. 12 Knowledge map Typed relationships connecting claims, instructions, attempts, and questions. 13 Verdict ledger A scoped judgment with reason, counterexample, correction, and later use. 14 Operating manual A usable route into the task, including interruption and resumption. 15 Portability drill Evidence about reconstruction, current instructions, and separately tested behavior. In the Fieldwork teaching case, the existing selector eventually points to `instructions-v3`. Earlier v1 and v2 records remain historical. A later explanation of the case should not silently change which instruction an earlier attempt used. The literal current instruction and selector are available in the distillation artifact.

title: System: demonstrate, deliver, and inspect the economics
text: Chapter Working document Carry forward 16 Capability demonstration A fresh task, first candidate, review, correction, effort, and bounded next responsibility. 17 Delegation contract Allowed sequence, required inputs, returned objects, repair limit, and escalation. 18 Review policy What a person checks, the source of their judgment, and how a mistaken verdict is repaired. 19 System contracts Matching job, source, candidate, and comparison identities across handoffs. 20 Enterprise runbook Intake, scoped delivery, support, capacity, maintenance, and recovery. 21 Product experiment Buyer question, offer, response, delivery, feedback, and the limits of the result. 22 Unit economics Revenue and cash assumptions, owner effort, fixed costs, capacity, and a changed case. 23 Capability portfolio Claims tied to actual evidence and the next missing demonstration. 24 Solo-enterprise plan A bounded sequence of next decisions under explicit commercial and personal constraints.

title: Work without coding
text: Use ordinary documents, folders, and a table. Read the instruction, attempt the task, compare the result with the source, record your judgment, and reopen the saved record. You can rehearse role handoffs sequentially. Label that as manual practice; it does not establish autonomous execution by a system you have not run. The optional memory checker demonstrates file integrity against a supplied manifest. The economics calculator performs arithmetic on explicit scenario inputs. Neither is required to understand or complete the core exercise. Their guides describe prerequisites, sample inputs, expected outputs, and what a successful run establishes.

title: Return to a stalled project
text: Open the latest decision and the evidence it cites. Identify the uncertainty that prevents the next useful action. If the current instruction is missing, repair the route to it. If the output violates a present rule, inspect the attempted application. If the offer has no buying evidence, choose an appropriate commercial inquiry. A different kind of gap calls for a different next action. Retain a short record of your decision, what you will do, and what result would change it. The value of this collection is that it lets you resume the inquiry without reconstructing your entire history or pretending that every unresolved question has already been answered.

title: Glossary
text: These definitions explain how terms are used in this book. They are reading aids, not a replacement for the sources and qualifications in the linked chapters. Term Meaning in the book Read further ACAI Accumulated Curiosity with Artificial Intelligence: the inquiry, practice, and retained judgment developed throughout the book. Chapter 7 Acceptance criteria Properties you can inspect to decide whether a particular result meets its stated purpose. Chapter 4 Agent A system that can carry out an authorized sequence using available tools and context; capabilities and autonomy depend on the actual implementation. Chapter 17 Artifact A document, example, script, diagram, or other inspectable object produced or used in the work. Practice index Capability An operation you can perform and support with appropriate evidence under stated conditions. Chapter 16 Capacity The amount of work that fits within stated time or resource constraints; it does not establish demand. Chapter 22 Claim A statement whose support, uncertainty, and intended use can be examined. Chapter 2 Context Information available to a model or person during a particular task. Available context and durable storage are different things. Chapter 8 Current selector A record or route identifying the instruction or artifact currently applicable to the task. Chapter 11 Distillation Turning examined material into a concise, scoped record while preserving the evidence and conditions needed to use it correctly. Chapter 11 Evaluation Comparing an actual result with relevant criteria and evidence; different evaluations support different claims. Chapter 18 Evidence Material or observations that support a particular claim within a stated scope. Naming a file does not establish what it contains. Chapter 2 Fieldwork Maya's fictional workshop-design business used for the running examples. Its conversations, outputs, and financial numbers are authored teaching material. Chapter 21 First principles Foundational relationships or premises used to explain a problem, whose applicability still requires examination. Chapter 5 Handoff Transfer of a defined responsibility and the required objects to another role or stage. Chapter 19 Hypothesis A proposed explanation or expectation that can be investigated and revised in light of evidence. Chapter 3 Knowledge graph Entities connected by specified relationships; the book begins with a small manual map. Chapter 12 Memory Retained information and judgment, together with the routes and rules that make it available for later work. Storage alone does not prove correct reuse. Chapter 8 Owner-time allowance Hours of owner work multiplied by an explicitly assumed hourly value; a comparison input, not automatically a paid wage. Chapter 22 Polymathy Developing and connecting understanding across domains while respecting the limits of each comparison. Chapter 6 Portability The ability to move and reconstruct relevant work; readable files and successful task behavior require separate evidence. Chapter 15 Provenance The origin and history needed to understand where a record came from and what supports it. Chapter 10 Source fidelity Preserving what the supplied evidence establishes, including uncertainty, rather than making the result merely look complete. Chapter 11 Sovereignty Meaningful control over the direction, authority, records, and dependencies of your work; not the absence of all external services. Chapter 15 SovMem The current TFIS name used for its intended sovereign-memory infrastructure. The book's manual exercises do not by themselves deploy it. Chapter 9 SSA-CMM TFIS’s capability maturity model for solo systems architects, using the canonical TFIS homepage ladder: Task Operator; AI-Assisted Operator; Workflow Orchestrator; Agent Supervisor; Multi-Agent Architect; Sovereign Architect. Chapter 23 Synthetic specimen An authored input, output, or scene created to make practice inspectable. It is not an observed model run or market result. Chapter 1 TFIS The Future Is Solo, whose assets provide the primary philosophy and maturity-model context for the book. Chapter 1 Transfer Applying learning in a changed situation; the differences between situations affect what a successful example establishes. Chapter 16 Unit economics A model of the revenue, costs, and effort attributable to a clearly defined unit of an offer. Chapter 22 Verdict A scoped accept, reject, or rewrite judgment tied to a particular object, its evidence, and a reason. Chapter 13 Workflow An organized sequence of operations with defined inputs, outputs, and conditions for continuing or stopping. Chapter 17 For SSA-CMM naming and the variations used by *The Functional Life*, see the full treatment in Chapter 23 and the primary TFIS sources. The glossary uses the homepage labels consistently. (The Future Is Solo, n.d.-a; The Future Is Solo, n.d.-b)

title: Capability baseline
text: Use with Chapter 1: The Future Is Solo. This is a book-developed practice record for investigating L0 → L1 capability in one task. It does not certify an SSA-CMM level.

title: How to use it without code
text: Copy the blank record into a text document. Use a clock to note time; paste a saved prompt into an ordinary AI chat; keep each input, output, and review in your practice folder. Use synthetic notes or material you are authorized to share. You need no paid integration, API key, or automated external action.
