title: Worked sample: fictional Fieldwork
text: All inputs, outputs, and timings below illustrate the record. They are not measured customer results or files supplied by a real business. Create your own practice files when using the template. **Task:** Turn Maya's synthetic workshop-preparation notes into a short provisional design brief. **Project output:** `workshop-brief-v1`. **Observed context:** Repetition in Maya's fictional personal preparation practice; no evidence of demand for a paid service. **Manual baseline:** 40 illustrative minutes, including thinking, drafting, and review. Maya found defining an inspectable learner outcome harder than arranging the headings. **Acceptance criteria:** The brief distinguishes supplied facts from assumptions; identifies a proposed learner task or the information needed to define one; proposes an observable learner output; avoids invented interviews, outcomes, and confirmed audiences.

title: Worked prompt
text: Run Synthetic input / trial purpose Observed example defect or success Verdict Repair or retained check 1 Ordinary notes, broad initial request Invents learner confidence and activity preferences Rewrite Require input-grounded claims and explicit assumptions 2 Same notes, revised prompt Proposed outcome is only “understand the topic” Rewrite Request a learner output that can be inspected 3 New notes with several possible audiences Chooses an audience as if confirmed Rewrite Preserve unresolved audience choices 4 Notes deliberately omit learner task Names the gap and asks a focused question Accept Retain missing-information behavior 5 Another ordinary input, current prompt Preserves assumptions and proposes inspectable output Accept after small wording edit Review every future draft; vary inputs further **Illustrative final-attempt time:** 3 minutes input preparation + 1 minute waiting + 10 minutes checking + 8 minutes revising/filing = 22 minutes. **Comparison:** 40 − 22 = an 18-minute difference between the recorded durations. The inputs differ, so this is not yet evidence of time saved. Run a separate comparison using comparable scope and the same quality bar, retaining input difficulty and familiarity/order as limitations. If that comparison eventually supported an 18-minute saving and setup were 90 minutes, five comparable future uses would recover setup. The arithmetic is conditional, not a measured forecast. **Inspect the example:** The practice specimens supply an authored bad answer and correction, a missing-task input corresponding to row 4, and an input/output pair corresponding to row 5. These are constructed teaching examples, not transcripts of model runs. Create and retain your own files for all five actual attempts. **Supported statement within the fiction:** Maya can use a saved prompt to draft this kind of provisional brief and inspect it for the defects tested. Untested topics, autonomous delivery, customer value, and general reliability remain outside the claim.

title: Acceptance and repair
text: The record is usable when a reviewer can locate the input and output of each attempt, understand the quality bar, and trace a prompt change to an observed defect. The latest prompt must be saved outside the chat. Five rows alone do not pass this check. Common failure Repair “Bad answer” is the entire review Name the unsupported sentence or missing requirement and the evidence that exposes it Only generation time is recorded Include input preparation, review, repair, filing, and setup separately Five identical easy inputs Add a meaningfully different input and a missing-information case Practice results become a claim of customer demand Relabel practice; create a separate demand hypothesis Reader cannot judge the output Narrow the task or involve a knowledgeable reviewer before relying on it Close the documents and explain the task's purpose, two failure conditions, and one remaining uncertainty. Reopen them to check your explanation. Carry the actual unresolved claims into Chapter 2.

title: Workshop-brief practice specimens
text: Use with the capability baseline in Chapter 1 and claim-evidence ledger in Chapter 2. Every input and output below is an authored fictional teaching specimen. None is a transcript of an actual AI run, an interview, or evidence of customer demand. The set makes selected example verdicts inspectable; it does not substitute for running and retaining your own five attempts.

title: Annotated review
text: The input does not establish low confidence or an activity preference. Those statements must be removed or presented as hypotheses to investigate. “Understand effective follow-up” does not specify a performance the reviewer can inspect. The final sentence promises learner outcomes that the input and this drafting exercise cannot establish. A reviewer can identify these problems by comparing the answer with the supplied text. They do not need to know whether some real professionals lack confidence; the issue is that the answer presents an unsupported assertion as a fact about this proposed audience.

title: Constructed correction
text: The correction does not complete the workshop design. It preserves the gap that has to be resolved before a useful design can be specified.

title: Fourth input: missing-task variant
text: This specimen corresponds to the missing-information trial described in row 4 of the baseline example. An acceptable response identifies the missing task and asks a focused question, such as: “What should a participant be able to produce from a set of meeting notes?” It must not silently decide that the workshop has already selected that outcome. The observation supporting claim **C02** is narrow and inspectable: this supplied input explicitly leaves the learner task unspecified.

title: Fifth input and corrected output
text: This specimen corresponds to the ordinary-input trial described in row 5. It supplies additional information so the response can propose an inspectable output. The workshop remains hypothetical. A constructed acceptable output is: The answer retains the input's uncertainty and proposes something the reviewer can inspect. These properties support **C04**, limited to this constructed output and these requirements. They do not establish that any real model reliably produces it. A reader's own C04 record should point to their actual saved output, prompt version, input, and review.

title: Use the specimens actively
text: Before reading the annotated review, mark every sentence in the flawed response that goes beyond the input. Then write your own correction. Compare it with the supplied one and explain any difference you want to keep. Later, run your saved prompt with your own synthetic inputs and retain the results. Keep constructed examples, actual runs, and observed customer evidence visibly separate.

title: Claim-evidence ledger
text: Use with Chapter 2: The End of Knowledge Scarcity. This book-developed artifact connects claims to their support and to the decisions that depend on them.

title: No-code path
text: Copy the record into an ordinary document. Open source links in a browser and record the exact section you inspect. If your assistant cannot browse, supply short excerpts with source details. It can help compare the wording; you still check the original.

title: Blank reusable record
text: **Project / date / owner:** **Decision this ledger serves:**

title: Claim [identifier]
text: Exact wording: Type: observation / empirical claim / interpretation / hypothesis / proposed action / preference Definition or narrower version, if needed: Source author or organization: Title / date / full reference: Source URL or local evidence file: Exact location inspected: Reading depth: full relevant passage / abstract only / identified but unread / own observation What the evidence establishes: What it does not establish: Status: supported as written / narrower support / contradicted / unresolved Decision affected: Next check / owner / stopping condition: Revision history: Repeat for each consequential claim. Keep observation records and public-source references distinct. A missing source is a reason to mark uncertainty, not to invent bibliographic details.

title: Verification queue
text: Claim Next observable check Evidence needed Owner Decision held provisional

title: Worked sample: fictional Fieldwork
text: The business observations and decisions below are fictional. The cited journal study is real. The example keeps these evidence types separate.

title: C01 — Demand for the proposed service
text: **Claim:** Independent educators need help turning a topic into a task a learner can perform and would value outside help. **Type/status:** Commercial hypothesis; unresolved. **Evidence:** None from customers. Maya's fictional preparation difficulties do not demonstrate customer demand. **Decision:** Whether to develop Fieldwork's proposed service beyond a practice brief. **Next check:** Prepare questions about an educator's actual design work and alternatives; later investigate with real people under appropriate consent. Do not report a conversation that has not occurred.

title: C02 — Missing detail in a practice input
text: **Claim:** The deliberately incomplete synthetic notes in Chapter 1's fourth trial do not specify a learner task. **Type/status:** Observation within the fictional practice; check against the exact input. **Evidence location:** Fourth input: missing-task variant. In your own ledger, substitute the actual input file and review. **Decision:** Ask a focused question before selecting an activity. **Limit:** This establishes a property of one synthetic input, not a pattern among actual educators.

title: C03 — A research claim and a separate design inference
text: **Original claim:** Adding a quiz makes any short workshop more effective. **Status:** Wording exceeds the cited evidence; revise. **Source:** Roediger, H. L., III, & Karpicke, J. D. (2006). Test-enhanced learning: Taking memory tests improves long-term retention. *Psychological Science, 17*(3), 249–255. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9280.2006.01693.x **Location/read depth:** Publisher abstract and bibliographic panel; abstract-only check. **Narrower support:** The experiments compare recall testing with restudy for students learning prose, with different patterns on immediate and delayed retention tests. **Separate practical inference:** Consider testing a recall attempt where retained information matters to the intended workshop task. **Unestablished:** Any general claim that Maya's workshop improves workplace performance, all quiz formats, or all learner groups. **Next check:** Identify what learners need to remember and what they need to demonstrate before choosing the activity.

title: C04 — Prompt behavior in a bounded attempt
text: **Claim:** The fifth fictional practice output preserves assumptions and an observable proposed learner output. **Type/status:** An inspectable result of that illustrated attempt. **Evidence location:** Fifth input and corrected output, an authored teaching specimen. In your own ledger, point to your actual saved input, output, and review. **Limit:** Does not establish that all future outputs pass or that delivery can run without review. **Decision:** Continue assisted drafting with human checking and varied inputs.

title: C05 — A working preference
text: **Claim:** Fieldwork should prioritize inspectable learner outcomes over polished slide counts. **Type/status:** Proposed operating preference, owned by Maya. **Reason:** It directs attention toward the usefulness she wants to investigate. **Limit:** A preference is not a research effect, customer testimonial, or universal rule for every workshop. **Next check:** Examine whether the preference makes the next design decision clearer; revise when the task requires it.

title: Acceptance criteria
text: The record is ready when another reader can locate at least one original outside source, repeat the supporting-passage check, distinguish observation from simulation, and identify which decisions remain provisional. Every consequential unsupported claim has a next action or is removed from the draft. An unresolved entry can be an acceptable outcome when its limitation is visible.

title: Common failures and repairs
text: Failure Repair Link opens but supports only the general topic Find the relevant passage; narrow or remove the claim Several summaries treated as independent studies Trace them to original sources and identify overlap Source reported as fully read when only abstract available Correct reading depth; remove unsupported detail Simulated persona treated as a customer Relabel simulation and preserve demand as untested Research finding merged with a recommendation Write two sentences and identify the application as your decision Ledger grows without changing any decision Keep the decision field; defer interesting but nonessential claims Close the ledger and explain one claim, its support, its limitation, and its practical consequence. Compare your explanation with the record. Bring the most important unresolved question to Chapter 3.

title: Curiosity map
text: Use this record to choose an inquiry that can change a piece of work. It is a book-developed practice artifact, not an official SSA-CMM assessment. Paper, a document editor, or a plain-text file works.

Mark untested audience claims as hypotheses.

title: Worked sample: fictional Fieldwork case
text: **Project:** Fieldwork; design practice, not customer research. **Current output:** `workshop-brief-v1`, linked to `claim-evidence-ledger-v1`. **Parent attempt:** The fifth practice specimen proposed an action-list task and provisional checking criteria. Its activity still needs to give each learner an actual opportunity to attempt that task. **Proposed benefit:** Help an independent educator specify a useful learner task. This remains a business hypothesis; no demand has been observed. Question Decision it could change What Maya observed in the fictional practice What remains unknown Evidence needed Will the proposed activity produce an action list that someone can check against the commitments in the notes? The activity and its connection to the proposed task The fifth specimen names an action-list task and candidate criteria; the activity remains undecided Whether the activity requires an individual attempt and exposes the distinctions in the criteria Inspect synthetic notes, a candidate activity, and an action-list attempt Do independent educators seek help defining learner tasks? Whether to pursue the service idea No customer evidence yet Actual preparation difficulties and willingness to seek help Future consent-based conversations about real preparation work Would a digital form simplify preparation? Whether to add a tool No repeated form-related bottleneck established Whether a form would save effort at an acceptable standard Repeated manual preparation records, then a bounded comparison if warranted **Selected question:** Will the proposed activity produce an action list that someone can check against the commitments in the notes? **Why now:** The answer can improve the brief using material Maya can create and inspect herself. **Alternative postponed:** A market inquiry matters, but synthetic design work cannot substitute for real educator evidence. Maya will prepare for that inquiry separately. **Starting expectation:** Requiring an individual action-list attempt will make the relationship between the activity and the proposed outcome easier to inspect. **Input:** Invented meeting notes containing a commitment, a suggestion, and an agreement with an unspecified owner. **Output:** A proposed activity, a practice input, and a check that applies the existing candidate criteria to an actual action-list attempt. **Boundary:** An illustrative forty-minute preparation session; no outside communication or real personal data. **Stopping condition:** Maya can show whether the check detects an unsupported owner or deadline, or name the specific distinction she still needs to understand. **Counterexample:** The revised outcome still permits an exercise with no learner action-list attempt. **Cannot establish:** Learner improvement, educator demand, optimal workshop duration, or business viability. **Observed result in the fictional case:** A discussion-only activity could cover the topic without producing an individual action list. A clean set of notes would also leave the distinction between suggestions and commitments untested. **Inspectable contrast:** Discussion-only: “Discuss what makes follow-up useful.” Revised activity: “Individually turn the supplied notes into an action list, then compare the result with the notes and candidate criteria.” The inquiry-brief specimen supplies the ambiguous notes and faulty answer used to test this revision. **Revision:** Carry the existing owner/date and commitment/suggestion criteria into the inquiry brief; use ambiguous notes and require an individual attempt before comparing answers. **Next inquiry:** How should the brief connect the learner task, actual attempt, and acceptance criteria? Record it in `inquiry-brief-v1`. **Parked question:** Could a digital form help assemble practice examples? **Return condition:** Revisit only if repeated manual work identifies example assembly as a meaningful bottleneck.

title: Acceptance criteria
text: Another reader can locate the unfinished work and the parent attempt. Every serious candidate question points to a decision, rather than only a topic. Observations, assumptions, and missing evidence remain distinguishable. The selected inquiry uses an evidence route appropriate to the claim. The result changes the work or explains precisely why it cannot yet change. A parked question has a return condition, and a next inquiry has a reason to exist. Without the assistant, you can explain why you chose this question and what the attempt cannot prove.

title: Common failure and repair
text: **Failure:** The map becomes a long collection of interests, tools, and reading links. **Repair:** Return to the unfinished output. Keep the questions that could alter its next revision. Move unrelated interests into open exploration without treating them as project obligations. **Failure:** A synthetic example is recorded as proof of customer need. **Repair:** Relabel it as design practice. Preserve the market question and specify the external evidence required to investigate it. **Failure:** The session repeatedly runs past its boundary. **Repair:** Reduce the promised output or choose a preparatory question. Record what remains unresolved instead of removing the stopping condition. Return to Chapter 3.

title: Inquiry brief
text: Create a record that a person or assistant can use without reading your previous conversation. This is a book-developed practice artifact. The core exercise needs no code or paid account.

title: Blank reusable template
text: **Inquiry name, version, and date:** **Parent question or attempt:** **Project output this inquiry should improve:** **Question:** **Situation:** Who is doing what, under which conditions? **Decision to make:** **My answer before assistance:** **Competing explanation or alternative:** **What I expect to observe:** **Evidence that would change my mind:** **Available inputs and source locations:** **Missing evidence:** **Allowed use of the inputs:** **Output requested:** **Acceptance criteria:** **How to handle missing information:** **What this inquiry will not establish:** **Time, scope, and stopping condition:**

title: Attempt record
text: **What I did, and whether assistance was used:** **Input version:** **Output location:** **What passed the criteria:** **What failed, with a specific example:** **Revision and its reason:** **Fresh example used to check the revision:** **What I can explain without the assistant:** **Error I can recognize without the assistant:** **Unresolved claims and ledger location:** **Next question:**

title: Worked sample: fictional Fieldwork case
text: **Name:** `inquiry-brief-v1`. **Parent:** The learner-task branch of `curiosity-map-v1`. **Output:** Revise `workshop-brief-v1` while preserving uncertainties in `claim-evidence-ledger-v1`. **Question:** What changes would make this synthetic action-list activity practice the stated learner task and expose unsupported additions? **Situation:** Maya is designing a provisional thirty-minute workshop example. Its proposed adult learners would turn meeting notes into action lists. No workshop has been delivered and no customer need has been validated. **Decision:** Whether the brief needs a corresponding practice input and checking criteria in addition to a clearer learner outcome. **Starting answer:** Maya has provisional criteria from her own earlier inspection. Replacing “understand effective follow-up” with a specific action-list outcome may be enough to guide a fresh draft without carrying those criteria into its instructions. **Alternative:** Better wording alone may leave the activity and review criteria unspecified. **Evidence that would change the answer:** An agenda can use the revised outcome while never asking a learner to produce an action list; a polished list can pass a vague check while adding unsupported commitments.

title: Synthetic input
text: The facilitator agreed to circulate the notes by Friday. The group suggested asking the venue about access arrangements; nobody was assigned. The group agreed to try a shorter introduction at the next session; no owner was assigned. **Available evidence:** These invented notes, Maya's draft, and her comparison of input with output. **Missing evidence:** Actual educator problems, learner attempts, delivery results, and willingness to pay. **Requested output:** Revised practice instructions, a candidate action list, and a check against the notes. **Criteria:** Preserve agreed actions; retain only stated owners and deadlines; separate suggestions from commitments; flag missing execution details; require a learner attempt before showing a completed answer. **Missing-information rule:** Leave the gap visible and identify a useful clarification. Do not invent an owner, deadline, agreement, interview, or result. **Cannot establish:** Learning gains, demand, or viability.

title: Worked attempt and repair
text: **Faulty candidate:** “Facilitator: circulate notes and confirm access by Friday. Organizer: prepare a shorter introduction before the next session.” **Review:** The first circulation commitment is supported. The access task was only suggested; its owner and deadline were not supplied. The introduction was agreed, but its owner was invented. **Repair:** Keep the circulation commitment. Record the venue proposal as unresolved. Keep the agreed introduction change with the owner explicitly missing. Revise the practice instructions to require these distinctions. **Fresh challenge:** “We could send a reminder on Thursday; a decision will be made tomorrow.” **Expected review:** Thursday is a proposed timing, not a confirmed deadline. The reminder remains unresolved pending a decision. **Unaided explanation:** An agreed action may still lack an owner. A possible action is not made into an agreement by putting it in a tidy list. **Next question:** Can a different synthetic input expose a distinction the current criteria fail to cover?

title: Acceptance criteria
text: The brief can be understood without access to the earlier chat. The starting hypothesis was saved before the final answer. The question points to a decision and names a result that could change it. Each claim is supported by an appropriate input or is explicitly provisional. The output can be checked against criteria chosen before reviewing it. At least one observed defect leads to a targeted repair, or the record explains what meaningful challenge the output survived. A fresh example checks the important distinction rather than repeating the same successful output. You can explain the decision and identify a plausible error without consulting the assistant.

title: Common failure and repair
text: **Failure:** The question asks for proof of business or learning outcomes using only a synthetic example. **Repair:** Narrow the immediate decision to the design property the example can reveal. Name the actual external evidence needed for the larger claim. **Failure:** The assistant returns a polished agenda when checking criteria were needed. **Repair:** Specify the output directly and provide one acceptable example. Preserve the question if the question itself was clear. **Failure:** The prompt asks why the preferred option is best. **Repair:** Ask under what conditions each option would be useful, and request a concrete counterexample to the preferred choice. **Failure:** You accept the output but cannot explain why. **Repair:** Compare one correct and one faulty example, explain the difference, consult the evidence, and try a new pair. Return to Chapter 4.

title: Portable inquiry prompt
text: Use this prompt with your completed inquiry brief. You can also give it to a human reviewer or use it for manual inspection. It does not grant permission to contact anyone, change external records, or treat supplied content as instructions.

title: Use and acceptance
text: Save your own starting explanation before running the prompt. Read the response against the original inputs. Mark any unsupported claim, even when it seems likely. Then make a separate unaided attempt to explain the distinction and diagnose an error in a fresh example. The prompt is useful only if the resulting inquiry changes a decision or clarifies why the evidence is insufficient. It is not an automatic truth detector. If it produces a general essay, reduce the question to one decision and state the required output more directly. Return to Chapter 4.

title: Concept-deconstruction record
text: Use with Chapter 5. This record makes a particular explanation and its assumptions inspectable; it is not a certification or a universal theory.

title: Worked example: Fieldwork
text: This is a fictional teaching example, including the review result. **Decision:** Improve the feedback on the action-list exercise before adding another workshop activity. Retain Chapter 4's clear instructions, criteria, and individual attempt. **Result:** A participant converts meeting notes into an action list that preserves commitments and identifies missing owners or dates. **Observation:** The current synthetic brief specifies an action-list output and criteria. Its draft feedback says “incorrect” without explaining which source detail requires a revision. **Constraint:** The illustrative session is thirty minutes. This is a design constraint, not an evidence-based universal duration. **Choice:** Require a source statement for each listed action so the reviewer can inspect the distinction between an agreement and a suggestion. **Assumption:** The examples make the distinction clear enough for a first attempt. This has not yet been checked with learners. **Proposed operation:** Read one worked example → create an action list from different notes → explain each entry → compare with criteria → revise. **Weak connection:** A correctness verdict does not yet tell the participant why an entry needs revision or how to apply the reason to another set of notes. **Check:** Give a peer the notes, a faulty action list, and the feedback. Ask what to change and which source detail justifies the change. **Illustrative result:** The peer recognizes the invented owner but interprets the feedback as a rule to remove every action that has no named owner. **Revision:** Explain that an agreed action can remain with its owner marked unknown. Point to the sentence recording the agreement, then check the explanation with different synthetic notes. **Limit:** This check can reveal whether the feedback communicates a usable reason to this reviewer. It does not establish general learning effectiveness, customer demand, or the appropriate workshop price.

title: Prompt for reviewing your explanation
text: Replace the bracketed fields and include your own attempted explanation first.

title: Acceptance and repair
text: The record is usable when another reader can identify the result, follow the proposed operations, find an unresolved assumption, and connect a recorded observation to your revision. Keep the first version so the change is visible. If the explanation consists mainly of broad terms, replace one term with an operation and its input/output. If the check cannot change the decision, choose a more consequential assumption. If you used simulated feedback, label it and arrange a real observation before relying on it as evidence about people.

title: Connection map
text: Use with Chapter 6: The Polymath Advantage. The map is a book-developed practice for testing an adaptation across domains. It is not a validated measure of transfer or a claim of generalist superiority.

title: No-code instructions
text: Copy the blank record into an ordinary document. Place the source situation and the target problem beside each other. Describe a relationship, then construct a small example that could show where the adaptation fails. You can review the example by reading it; no software testing framework is required.

title: Worked sample: fictional Fieldwork
text: Maya is designing a synthetic thirty-minute workshop in which adult learners convert meeting notes into an action list. No learner performance or customer demand is established by this design exercise. **Target difficulty:** Detect invented commitments, owners, and deadlines while allowing faithful paraphrases. **Source idea:** Evaluate whether an output satisfies meaningful requirements rather than only matching one reference sentence. **Relevant engineering source:** Grace, M., Hadfield, J., Olivares, R., & De Jonghe, J. (2026, January 9). *Demystifying evals for AI agents*. Anthropic. https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents **Inspected location:** “Types of graders for agents,” including limitations of exact checks, and “Design graders thoughtfully.” The source is engineering guidance about AI systems. The workshop adaptation is Maya's design proposal, not a tested finding from that article. Source operation Workshop counterpart Useful relationship Mismatch Defined input Synthetic meeting notes Review has evidence to compare with output Real notes may omit shared context Requirement Only agreed actions are commitments Check meaning rather than appearance Ambiguity may require a question Output condition Named owners and deadlines need support Detect plausible invented detail Missing information can be validly flagged Review verdict Reason tied to a note Shows why a response needs revision Learners also need a chance to explain and retry **Rejected part of the analogy:** Treating a single model answer as the only valid output; treating a pass as proof of learning transfer.

title: Plausible defective output
text: **Review:** First item is supported. Second converts a suggestion into an assigned commitment and invents the coordinator. Third preserves an agreed change but invents the owner and Thursday deadline.

title: Valid variation
text: Both “The facilitator will circulate the notes no later than Friday” and “Owner: facilitator; action: circulate notes; due: Friday” preserve the first line's meaning. An exact-wording check would be inappropriate if it rejected one solely for its expression.

title: Boundary case
text: For “We could ask the venue; let's return to that,” the review should preserve an unresolved proposal. It should not infer agreement or assign an owner just to complete a table.

title: Revision discovered by testing the check
text: **Defective review rule:** Every action must have an owner. **Repair:** Show whether ownership is established. An agreed action with no stated owner should flag the missing assignment. It is not ready for execution until the relevant person resolves it; a drafting tool must not invent the resolution. **Decision:** Keep the adapted comparison for further practice, permitting faithful variation and explicitly representing uncertainty. Add the review rule to the current brief and instructions. Do not claim learner outcomes, customer value, or general reliability.

title: Acceptance criteria
text: The record is usable when another reader can identify the source relationship, the target decision, one consequential mismatch, and a trial that could have rejected the adaptation. The current decision must be tied to an observed example. A rejected connection may pass the exercise if the evidence explains why it should not be used.

title: Common failures and repairs
text: Failure Repair Connection is only “both are systems” Name the specific dependency or operation being compared Impressive source terminology replaces an explanation Explain the relationship in ordinary words and verify the source meaning Test rejects valid output variation Change the criterion to the property that matters Rule forces a complete-looking answer Distinguish required knowledge from a permitted uncertainty flag Successful desk review becomes a learning claim Limit the result to design evidence; investigate learner performance separately Target consequences exceed your expertise Narrow the trial or obtain informed review before relying on it Close the map and explain the connection without its technical label. Apply it to a changed case, such as an imprecise deadline. Record whether the relationship still helps and where it stops.

title: Learning-loop record
text: Use with Chapter 7: The Accumulated Curiosity Loop. This is a human-led, book-developed practice for making inquiry and correction repeatable. It does not establish autonomous learning or certify an SSA-CMM level.

title: No-code instructions
text: Keep the record in an ordinary document. Link the actual input, current instruction, output, and review. Start the second pass from those saved materials. Reopen edited files to check that your change exists, and inspect whether the next output uses it. No agent platform or automated write is required.

title: Blank reusable record
text: **Project / owner:** **Current procedure file and version:** **Current working artifact:** **Relevant prior artifacts:** **Human review required at:** **What the assistant is allowed to do:** **Conditions that stop the work for clarification:**

title: Pass [identifier and date]
text: **Question:** What uncertainty affects which decision? **Starting understanding:** Write your own explanation before asking for help. **Evidence inspected:** List source or practice files, exact locations, and limits. **Proposed change:** What should behave differently, and why? **Test:** Input: Current instruction/version actually supplied: Expected properties: Plausible failure: Review method: Stopping condition: **Observed result:** Link the output and identify the relevant passage or behavior. **Verdict:** Accept / revise / reject / unresolved, with a specific reason. **Application:** Which working file changed, and how did you verify the saved change? **Next question:** **What remains unestablished:**

title: Second-pass reuse check
text: Prior correction this pass should use: Saved location where this correction is current: Different input or new task instance: Evidence that the correct version was supplied: Result showing reuse or recurrence of the defect: Diagnosis if the defect recurs: Next action:

title: Worked sample: fictional Fieldwork
text: **Current project:** The synthetic thirty-minute meeting-notes-to-action-list workshop. **Working artifact:** `workshop-brief-v1`. **Prior records:** Capability baseline; `claim-evidence-ledger-v1`; `curiosity-map-v1`; `inquiry-brief-v1`; concept-deconstruction record; `connection-map-v1`. **New cumulative record:** `learning-loop-v1`. Its first lines point to the current instruction and review sheet, illustrated by the current-version entry in the constructed practice packet. Earlier drafts remain identifiable as history.

title: Pass run-01 — Get the correction into the working instruction
text: **Question:** Can a fresh attempt preserve an agreed action with missing ownership using saved materials alone? **Starting diagnosis:** An old prompt still demands complete action details. The current review sheet allows an honest missing-owner flag. The two materials disagree. **Explanation:** Agreement and readiness to execute are different conditions. The instruction must preserve an agreement while showing which required details remain unsettled. **Proposed change:** Reconcile the current prompt with the review sheet; supply it in a fresh practice conversation. The intermediate version shows an incomplete migration: the owner rule is restored but an old deadline instruction remains. **Test input:** Synthetic notes include one explicit commitment, a suggestion, and an agreed change with an unassigned owner. **Expected properties:** Preserve supported commitments; do not promote suggestions; flag missing owners and deadlines without inventing details. **Observed fictional result:** The first constructed output flags the owner gap but invents a deadline for the suggested venue inquiry. **Verdict:** Revise. The response improved one field but still violates the evidence boundary for another. **Application:** Compare the actual supplied instruction with the existing review sheet. Remove the old deadline suggestion and restore the already-accepted requirement; retain the failed output. The corrected version preserves both owner and deadline boundaries. Reopen saved files before starting again. **Unestablished:** Customer demand, real learner outcomes, autonomous delivery, and general reliability.

title: Pass run-02 — Check reuse on a changed input
text: **Prior correction:** Owners and deadlines require support; missing or imprecise details must remain visible. **Changed input:** An agreed action has a deadline described only as “soon.” **Expected property:** Preserve the imprecision or flag that a precise date is not specified. Do not invent a calendar date. **Procedure:** Open the current-version pointer, load the saved instruction, supply the new input, and compare the output with the notes. **Illustrative successful result:** The second constructed output keeps “soon” as the stated timing and asks for a precise date before treating the assignment as scheduled. **Verdict:** Accept the bounded behavior in this synthetic case. Preserve the output and rule; continue human review. **Next question:** What should the procedure do when notes contain a genuine contradiction? Investigate only if that input belongs in the intended scope; otherwise define a clarification stop. The entries illustrate the method. Readers must retain their own actual files and may observe different results. Do not use the fictional pass as a reliability statistic.

title: Acceptance criteria
text: The record is usable when a reviewer can trace an uncertainty to evidence, evidence to a changed working instruction, and that instruction to a second attempt. The correct current version must be identifiable. Human decisions, assistant actions, and unresolved questions must be distinguishable. A second pass that repeats a defect can still complete the exercise if the failure and broken handoff are documented. Claim improvement only when the recorded output supports it.

title: Common failures and repairs
text: Failure Repair Interesting explanation never changes the work Identify the decision and update the relevant artifact, or retain the finding as background Review says only “better” Name the expected property, observed behavior, and evidence Current and obsolete instructions conflict Mark one current entry point and move superseded instructions to clearly labeled history Next pass never reads the correction Link and supply the saved current requirement before drafting Model praises its own output without a check Compare with the actual input, source, or an independent review criterion Every failure creates a larger prompt Diagnose version, conflicting examples, scope, and handoffs before adding text Record becomes harder to maintain than the task Keep question, evidence, tested change, verdict, and next action, with links to underlying files After an interval, explain the retained rule without opening the answer and apply it to a changed example. Use any gap to choose the next small practice. The schedule is yours to adapt; this record does not prescribe an experimentally validated review interval.

title: Two-pass practice packet
text: Every instruction, input, and response below is **authored teaching material for the fictional Fieldwork case**, not a transcript of a real model run. There are no tool receipts or measured performance rates. Compare these specimens yourself, then retain actual records when performing your own exercise. The immediate output is an example action list used to check the design of `workshop-brief-v1`; it is not evidence that a learner has completed the workshop.

title: Current-version entry
text: An illustrative `learning-loop-v1` entry: Current drafting instruction: v2. Current review criteria: review sheet. Previous failed attempt: run-01. Changed-input reuse check: run-02. Reason for the revision: migration diagnosis. The instruction governs the next attempt. The history explains it. A link to the failed attempt does not make its instruction current again.

title: Obsolete instruction v0
text: Both requirements can encourage invented details. Previous chapters already rejected them as standards for a faithful action list.

title: Intermediate instruction v1
text: The owner correction reached this document. The deadline correction did not. This explicit conflict supports diagnosing an incomplete migration. It does not prove how a real model would respond.

title: Review sheet
text: Each agreed action must have support in the notes. Keep suggestions separate from agreements. Owners and deadlines must come from the notes; preserve missing or imprecise details. Give a short source-based reason for any correction. Judge meaning, allowing faithful paraphrases. These requirements carry forward the existing decisions from Chapters 4–6.

title: Run-01 input and flawed output
text: **Instruction supplied:** the intermediate v1 above. **Synthetic input:** **Constructed flawed output:** Status Item Owner Timing Source Agreed Circulate the notes Facilitator Friday 1 Suggestion Ask the venue about access Unspecified Wednesday 2 Agreed Shorten the next introduction Unspecified Unspecified 3 The second row remains a suggestion, but its Wednesday timing has no support. Keeping the status correct does not make the invented date acceptable.

title: Review and migration diagnosis
text: **Verdict:** Revise the example; reject the unsupported Wednesday date. **Evidence:** Input line 2 contains no date. The supplied v1 still asks for practical deadlines, while the review sheet forbids invention. The requirements conflict. **Repair:** Remove the obsolete deadline instruction and restore the existing evidence boundary. The corrected second row reads: suggestion; ask the venue about access; owner unspecified; timing unspecified; source 2. **Working change:** The proposed workshop brief uses that distinction in its example answer and retains an individual attempt before comparison. Its existing learner task does not change. Record v2 as current; keep v1 attached to this history. In your real exercise, reopen the edited instruction and confirm what was saved. This specimen does not claim a tool wrote or verified a file.

title: Run-02 changed input and reviewed output
text: **Instruction supplied:** current v2, reached through the entry above. **Synthetic input:** **Constructed reviewed output:** Status Item Owner Timing Source Agreed Send the revised worksheet Facilitator Soon; precise date unspecified 1 Suggestion Ask another educator for examples Unspecified Unspecified 2 **Clarification:** Line 1 establishes an agreement and an owner, but “soon” cannot determine a calendar date. Confirm a precise date before treating this as a scheduled commitment. Line 2 does not authorize contacting anyone. **Verdict:** Accept the displayed example under the review sheet. Its owner and timing fields preserve the supplied evidence. It illustrates how the saved correction applies to a changed input; it establishes neither actual model reliability nor a learner outcome. **Next unresolved case:** Notes that contain conflicting dates for the same commitment. Preserve both statements and seek clarification; the examples above do not settle that conflict.

title: Use this packet
text: Before reading the verdicts, mark each unsupported field yourself. Then compare v1 and v2 and explain which existing decision failed to reach the intermediate document. For your own two passes, save actual inputs and outputs, note the supplied version, and record a failure honestly if it recurs. Merely copying the successful specimen cannot demonstrate reuse. Return to the learning-loop record or Chapter 7.

title: Memory Inventory
text: Use this with Chapter 8. Inventory the records needed for one recurring task and test what you can recover and use. This book-developed practice is not an official SSA-CMM assessment.

title: Blank reusable template
text: **Inventory name and revision:** **Task this working set supports:** **Next decision or output:** **Who will use these records:** **Material authorized for this exercise:** **Important unknowns:** Record Purpose and question it should answer Location or pointer Status: source, inference, decision, preference, or practice Current or historical role What would make it need review?                   A source record preserves what the source says; its label does not certify that the source is true. A historical failed attempt can remain valuable without becoming a current instruction.

title: Retrieval and use checks
text: Begin from a question about the task rather than an exact filename. Record the material actually available to the person or assistant doing the check. Question Starting location and route taken Material recovered Applicable status/version recognizable? Evidence or rationale recoverable? Fresh use check and observed result Limitation or repair               **What I should be able to explain without opening the records:** **What I may retrieve when needed:** **Where I need additional evidence or expertise:**

title: Verify one saved change
text: **Record changed and intended result:** **Actual saved location reopened:** **Wording and links inspected:** **What happened:** **Remaining limitation:**

title: Portability observation
text: **Can the selected records open outside the original application?** **Which links, comments, status labels, or other dependencies remain usable?** **What has not been checked?**

title: Fictional worked sample: Maya and Fieldwork
text: **Inventory:** `memory-inventory-v1`. **Task:** Prepare and review another version of the proposed thirty-minute workshop in which adults convert synthetic meeting notes into an action list. **Next decision:** Explain and apply the current evidence boundary without losing the reasons behind it. **User:** Maya, or a fresh assistant receiving selected synthetic material under Maya's direction. **Unknowns:** Customer need, willingness to pay, and learner outcomes remain untested. No real customer material is included. Record Purpose and question Working location or pointer Status Current or historical role Review trigger `workshop-brief-v1` What task is the proposed workshop meant to teach? Starting proposal and later working change Proposed design and labeled assumptions Current provisional brief Learner task or scope changes `claim-evidence-ledger-v1` Which claims are observed, inferred, chosen, or untested? Claims ledger Mixed, with individual status labels Current claim accounting New relevant evidence or public use of a claim `connection-map-v1` Why was “every action must have an owner” rejected? Connection map Historical proposal and reviewed reasoning History; rejected rule is clearly labeled Rationale proves unclear or task changes `learning-loop-v1` Which instructions apply now, and what did the later practice reveal? Chapter 7 entry and history, with later updates noted below Review history and pointer to current instructions Existing authority route remains intact Accepted instruction change or new failure Current drafting instructions and review sheet What should the next draft preserve and flag? Initial pointer; later Chapter 11 pointer Reviewed operating decision Current instruction; no duplicate introduced Accepted revision after a new observation Relevant synthetic inputs and practice outputs What did the owner and deadline examples actually contain? Run-01 and run-02 Synthetic sources and constructed practice outputs Evidence for a narrow design check Input changes or a different behavior needs testing `action-list-rule-rationale-v1` How do the owner, deadline, and “soon” examples explain the present rule? Worked rationale below Reviewed explanation with links Supports current instruction; does not replace it Current instruction or support changes

title: Fictional retrieval record
text: Question Route and result Repair or limitation Which drafting instructions apply now? Followed `learning-loop-v1`; recovered current instructions and review sheet. This route already worked at the end of Chapter 7. Why may an agreed action remain with an unspecified owner, and what did the deadline failure add? Current instruction was found. Recovering the full reason required separate searches through the connection map and loop history. Added `action-list-rule-rationale-v1` linking existing current instruction and relevant comparisons. Repeated the route and opened each link. What prevents “soon” from becoming an invented date? Followed the rationale to the changed practice example and the current evidence boundary. Supports this distinction; does not establish reliability for every kind of ambiguous note. **Fresh use check:** Supply the current instructions, rationale, brief, and synthetic reminder example: “We could send a reminder on Thursday; a decision will be made tomorrow.” Inspect whether Thursday remains proposed rather than becoming a confirmed deadline. Record the actual output when performing your own check; a supplied rule is not proof that an assistant followed it. **Unaided knowledge:** Maya should explain the difference between a suggestion and an agreement, and why a missing owner or imprecise deadline must remain visible. **Retrieved details:** Exact source wording, publication metadata, and the particular input/output pair used in a previous check. **Further evidence needed:** Real audience need and actual learner performance; the existing folder cannot supply evidence that was never collected. **Saved-change check:** Reopen `action-list-rule-rationale-v1`, confirm the current-instruction link and the links to owner/deadline comparisons, then follow the new inventory pointer. Preserve the current-version route in `learning-loop-v1`. **Portability status:** This inventory identifies which records need a move test. Chapter 9 performs a small test; listing a readable format here is not evidence that a complete working set has already been moved.

title: Worked rationale, with later updates
text: **Record:** `action-list-rule-rationale-v1`. **Role:** Explain the evidence boundary and connect its history. This record does not issue a competing task instruction. The specimens below are authored teaching material; readers must retain their own actual retrieval and write-check results. **Initial Chapter 8 rationale:** An agreement can exist without an assigned owner. Removing every unassigned item would hide agreed work; inventing an owner would misrepresent the notes. The connection-map example supplies the rejected completeness proposal and its repair. Keep the agreement and show the missing assignment. The same source boundary applies to timing. Run-01 contains an unsupported Wednesday date. Its migration diagnosis shows that an obsolete deadline suggestion remained in an intermediate instruction. The correction restores the existing requirement rather than discovering a new principle. Run-02 preserves “soon” and leaves the precise date unresolved. **Authority at the Chapter 8 point in the story:** The existing learning-loop entry selects v2. The rationale explains that instruction and its supporting examples. **Later update after Chapter 11:** The distillation record adds reviewed handling for contradictory deadlines with no established supersession. Preserve the shared action and owner, retain both timing claims, and seek clarification. The same logical current-version route now selects instructions-v3. The literal v3 instruction governs current main-case work; the v2 specimen remains historical. This is an explicit later addition to the living artifact, not a claim that Chapter 8 already performed Chapter 11's exercise. **Scope and limit:** These records support source-faithful representation in the fictional workshop-design practice. They do not authorize assigning work, contacting participants, selecting an unresolved date, or claiming customer/learner outcomes. **Review trigger:** A changed task instruction, corrected source, or a new case that reveals an omission. Revisit the explanation and links affected by that change; retain one current-instruction route.

title: Acceptance criteria
text: One task and its necessary records are identified. Retrieval questions concern the work, rather than only filenames. The current instruction can be distinguished from history and rejected proposals. At least one consequential rationale can be followed to relevant support. Retrieval and correct use have separate recorded outcomes. A saved change is reopened and its relevant links are checked. The inventory distinguishes unaided understanding, retrieved detail, and missing evidence. Results state their limits; one synthetic check is not a reliability rate.

title: Common failure and repair
text: Failure Repair A current instruction is findable, but its reason requires reconstructing several conversations. Add a concise linked rationale, keeping one authority route for the instruction. Search returns an older proposal without making its rejection clear. Mark its status where it appears and connect it to the current decision. A fresh output cites the rule but violates it. Inspect the supplied working set and the output; identify the specific conflict or error before adding more text. Three summaries of one paper are treated as three sources. Link to the inspected source and label derived summaries; preserve the claim's limits. The inventory contains the answer “somewhere,” with no usable location. Add a resolvable location or mark the record missing. A retrieval result is used to claim knowledge of a customer need. Check whether such evidence exists. Keep the claim untested when it does not. The new rationale becomes a second instruction with different wording. Restore one current instruction and let the rationale explain it through links.

title: Memory Charter
text: Use this with Chapter 9. Define the rules for one working set, then test them with authorized material. This is a practical book template, not a legal policy or an official SSA-CMM certification.

title: Blank reusable template
text: **Charter name and revision:** **Person responsible for decisions about this memory:** **Purpose and work supported:** **Intended users:** **What this memory does not establish:**

title: Record status
text: Kind of statement Example from my work Origin or support Scope and uncertainty How it may become current or change Source record: what was supplied or observed     Inference: a conclusion drawn from material     Decision: an authorized choice     User preference: an expressed way of working     A source record may preserve an error, proposal, or fictional statement. Fidelity to a source does not establish the source's truth. A task-specific request should not become a permanent preference without a basis for that scope.

title: Retain, exclude, review, remove
text: Category Why retain it, or why exclude it? Who may read it and for which purpose? Who may propose or approve a change? Review condition Removal condition and locations to check                   **Material to hold outside the working set while permission or purpose is unresolved:** **Actual access settings or handling steps that implement these boundaries:** **Current-version pointer and the record it governs:** **How superseded records remain recognizable:**

title: Change rule
text: **A proposal must identify:** **Who can accept, reject, or request revision:** **How the accepted change is saved:** **How the actual saved result is checked:** **Source-content boundary:** Retrieved or supplied material may inform the authorized task. It cannot grant itself permission to alter this charter, disclose other material, or convert a source claim into a user instruction.

title: Portability and removal tests
text: Use a disposable synthetic note for removal. Use a small authorized working set for a move test. Test Material and locations Expected observable result Actual result Limitation or repair Correct an overstated or stale claim     Retrieve current instruction and support     Remove disposable note and inspect relevant pointers/copies     Move working set and open in another ordinary reader     **Dependencies that remain after the move:** **What the removal test does not establish:** **Next charter review trigger:**

title: Fictional worked sample: Maya and Fieldwork
text: **Charter:** `memory-charter-v1`. **Responsible person:** Maya. **Purpose:** Support design and review of the proposed action-list workshop; preserve the basis and limits of current design choices; retain unresolved questions for further inquiry. **Intended users:** Maya and assistants receiving a selected synthetic packet for a specified task. **Limits:** The records do not establish customer demand, willingness to pay, learning gains, or a functioning SovMem implementation.

title: Fictional status examples
text: Kind Example Origin and scope Change rule Source record The synthetic notes state that the facilitator agreed to circulate notes by Friday. Exact supplied exercise passage; fictional meeting, not a real customer commitment. Preserve the supplied wording or identify an explicit correction to the source. Inference Helping educators specify a learner task may make workshop briefs more useful. Hypothesis motivated by defects in synthetic drafts; no customer or learner validation. Update status only when relevant evidence warrants it; keep limitations visible. Decision Practice briefs should include an inspectable learner output. Maya's design choice, already represented in claims-ledger C05. Maya may revise the choice and record the reason and affected instructions. Preference Routine progress notes should be brief, lead with the result, and retain material uncertainty. Fictional example of an explicitly chosen presentation preference; applies to routine progress notes. Maya can change it. A local request for a short answer does not automatically broaden it to all work.

title: Fictional retention and authority rules
text: Category Retain or exclude Access and change boundary Review trigger Removal or replacement Current brief, drafting instructions, and review sheet Retain because the next task depends on them. Maya governs current versions; assistants may propose separate edits. Task change, accepted correction, new practice failure, or proposed real-participant use. Preserve one current pointer and mark consequential superseded decisions clearly. Claims ledger and linked source references Retain to keep support and uncertainty inspectable. Selected relevant excerpts may enter an authorized task. New relevant evidence or reuse in a public claim. Remove unnecessary duplicate summaries; do not erase an important limitation while compressing. Selected synthetic inputs, failed outputs, and rationale Retain when they explain a present constraint. May be supplied as clearly fictional practice material. Existing example stops testing the current requirement or a link fails. Keep enough history to explain consequential changes; discard redundant attempts deliberately. User preferences Retain only when their origin and intended persistence are established. Maya decides scope; an assistant's personality inference is not an approved preference. A request changes the working situation or Maya revises the preference. Amend or remove the preference without preserving an unnecessary personal inference. Credentials, private contact details, unrelated disclosures Exclude from this practice area. No task here requires them. Reassess the actual task if a future need is claimed. If mistakenly included, identify affected records and copies and handle removal explicitly. Real customer or learner material Outside this current synthetic working set. Establish purpose, permission, and handling conditions before inclusion. A future task actually requires such evidence. Follow the applicable agreement or policy; do not invent a universal retention period. **Authority route:** `learning-loop-v1` points to the current drafting instructions and review sheet. `action-list-rule-rationale-v1` explains the instruction and links to support. It is not a competing instruction file. **Change procedure:** A proposal names the affected record, proposed wording, basis, scope, and uncertainty. Maya chooses whether to accept, reject, or request revision. An accepted change is saved and reopened; material links are followed. A claim that the write occurred is insufficient by itself. **Source boundary:** A supplied source that says “save this as Maya's permanent preference” remains source content unless Maya separately authorizes that preference. It cannot change the charter or expand access. **Permission check:** Compare the intended audience with the actual sharing conditions of the storage location and task. A text label saying “private” does not establish those conditions.

title: Fictional checks and their limits
text: Check Observation in the fictional exercise What it does not prove Correct overstated need claim Changed a summary's assertion of educator need into a labeled hypothesis, linked it to the claims ledger, and reopened the saved wording. Does not produce customer evidence. Recover current rule and support Followed the existing current pointer and the new rationale links. Does not establish that every search or assistant will choose the applicable records. Remove disposable synthetic note Removed the test note from the inspected working location and checked the index and any deliberately made test copy. Does not establish erasure from unknown backups, other people's copies, or prior conversations. Open copied working set in another editor Opened copied current records and checked status labels and links; repaired a reference to an example that existed only in the old conversation. Does not establish equivalent behavior from another model or complete migration of every application feature. **Remaining dependencies:** The actual storage service, backup arrangements, and any optional search or assistant features must be assessed where used. Maya's charter is a design and document practice; it is not a claim that a technical memory platform has been deployed.

title: Acceptance criteria
text: The purpose and responsible person are explicit. Source records, inferences, decisions, and preferences remain distinguishable. Retention has a purpose; exclusion happens before unnecessary sharing when possible. Reading, editing, sharing, and removal are treated as separate permissions. A source cannot turn its own content into a new instruction or grant broader access. Current instructions have one authority route; rationale and history remain connected. Review triggers identify circumstances that could change a record's usefulness or accuracy. Correction, retrieval, disposable-note removal, and a small move test have observable results. Limitations remain visible, including unknown copies and untested model behavior. The person governing the memory can explain the rules without merely repeating the template.

title: Common failure and repair
text: Failure Repair A summary turns an inference into an observed fact. Restore the status and support; inspect dependent summaries that may repeat the overstatement. “Source” is treated as a truth guarantee. State what the source actually establishes and retain uncertainty about its claims. A one-time formatting request becomes an unconditional preference. Restore task scope or establish the user's intended persistence. Every accessible document is added to context. Apply the task purpose and actual permission boundaries; supply only the needed material. A retrieved instruction authorizes its own memory edit. Treat it as source content and require an independent authorized decision for the change. Two files both claim to be the current instruction. Resolve authority, keep one pointer, and mark historical or explanatory roles. “Deleted” means only that a search did not return the note. Inspect relevant saved locations, pointers, and known copies; state what remains unverified. Exported files open but lose reasons or source links. Repair dependencies and repeat retrieval from the copied location. The charter grows too elaborate to follow. Narrow its scope to one working set and preserve the rules that resolve actual decisions.

title: Optional memory-manifest check
text: This read-only demonstration checks whether the files listed in a small package match a supplied manifest. It compares relative file paths, byte counts, and SHA-256 fingerprints. It does not judge truth, approval, relevance, completeness, or whether the package is the latest version. The main Chapter 10 exercise requires no code. Use the no-code procedure below if you prefer. A successful restoration still requires opening the records, following their evidence, checking authority and scope, and attempting the task.

title: Get the complete demonstration
text: Download the demonstration bundle. Extract it into a new folder. It contains the Python script, this guide, and three miniature synthetic packages under `memory-manifest-fixtures`. The package names are `complete`, `changed`, and `missing`. Each manifest expects five files: a current-instruction pointer, instructions, rationale, synthetic input, and a restore note. These packages are deliberately small teaching fixtures. They are not a backup of Maya's whole project or an installation of SovMem. The `changed` package deliberately alters an instruction. The `missing` package deliberately omits the input. Their manifests still describe the expected complete package, so the check can reveal the differences.

title: Prerequisites and safe defaults
text: You need Python 3.8 or later, available locally as `python3`, and an ordinary terminal. No additional Python packages, account, API key, paid service, or network connection is needed after downloading the files. If your computer uses a different Python command, substitute that command. The program does not write, repair, delete, upload, or execute the listed files. It reports their simple relative names without printing their contents. It rejects absolute paths, path traversal, symlinks, duplicate entries, malformed manifests, and oversized demonstration inputs. It accepts simple letters, digits, underscores, periods, hyphens, and slashes in listed paths. This is a local teaching tool for a stable folder you control. It is not hardened against a hostile process changing paths while the check runs. Do not treat its output as a security certification.

title: Run the complete package
text: Open a terminal in the extracted folder containing `check_memory_manifest.py`. Run: Expected output: An exit code is the number a program returns to describe how it finished. This successful comparison returns `0`.

title: Run the deliberately changed package
text: Expected output: This returns `1`, as intended. Open the changed instruction beside the complete package's instruction to inspect the difference. Do not “repair” it by changing the manifest merely to make the check pass. First establish which content you actually intend to retain.

title: Run the deliberately incomplete package
text: Expected output: This also returns `1`, as intended. The missing dependency prevents the package from supplying the input named by the rationale. The checker reports it but does not restore it. An invalid manifest, unsafe path, inaccessible file, or exceeded demonstration limit returns `2` and an error message. Review the manifest format and local files. The limits are 1 MiB of manifest data, 1,000 listed files, and 10 MiB per listed file. They keep this demonstration bounded; the tool is not a general backup application.

title: No-code equivalent
text: Open `memory-manifest-fixtures/complete/restore-note.md` in a text editor or Markdown reader. Follow its current-instruction link, then open the rationale and synthetic input. Write a list of the five expected files. Locate them in each package without using the original complete package as a hidden dependency. Compare the complete and changed instruction files. Identify the instruction that was replaced, and explain how its meaning changed. In the missing package, identify the absent synthetic input. Explain why a readable rationale without its evidence is insufficient for this recovery task. From the complete package, explain the applicable instruction and its reason. Try a fresh synthetic note that contains an unknown owner or imprecise deadline and inspect the output. This manual procedure checks meaning and usability. It is not a byte-for-byte fingerprint comparison. For a small bundle, it is a useful first restoration check whether or not you run the program.

title: What a match means
text: A match means the listed file's byte count and calculated fingerprint agree with the values in the supplied manifest. A file can match perfectly while containing a false claim or an obsolete instruction. Files omitted from the manifest are not checked. The program does not follow Markdown links or assess whether the listed set is sufficient for a task. The manifest is itself ordinary editable data. If someone changes both it and the files consistently, this comparison can pass. It does not authenticate who created the package or protect the expected values from alteration. Keep file consistency, record authority, semantic accuracy, and successful task reuse as separate results. Use your charter and human review to decide what belongs in the package. Use restoration to establish what can actually be recovered.

title: Verification performed for this book
text: The script was run with Python 3.11.3 against all three supplied packages. The complete package returned `0`; the changed and missing packages returned `1` and identified the intended file. Separate synthetic checks for path traversal, an absolute path, a symlink, a duplicate JSON key, and incorrect invocation returned `2`. File fingerprints before and after the runs confirmed that the staged demonstration files were unchanged. These results establish the stated checks in this local demonstration. They do not establish every possible failure mode or production suitability.

title: Memory lanes
text: Use this with Chapter 10 after completing your memory inventory and charter. The four roles are this book's practical arrangement, not an official SSA-CMM assessment or a scientific taxonomy. Begin with one authorized working set. Ordinary text files and folders are sufficient.

title: Fictional worked sample: Fieldwork
text: **Record:** `memory-lanes-v1`. Maya is developing a possible thirty-minute workshop in which adult learners convert supplied meeting notes into an action list. All practice inputs and results here are fictional and synthetic. No demand, customers, or learner benefits have been established. Role Illustrative location Contents and authority Working context `work/` Current task packet, fresh synthetic notes, instructions retrieved through the existing pointer, review criteria. No automatic lasting authority. Project workspace `projects/fieldwork/` `workshop-brief-v1`, `learning-loop-v1`, charter, inventory, rationale, evidence ledger, selected inputs/outputs. Candidate changes are visibly proposed. Reviewed durable memory `memory/` `commitment-evidence-principle-v1`, approved by Maya within its stated scope. It explains a principle and does not replace task instructions. Portable archive `archive/` Selected workshop-design snapshot, readable file list, approved-state description, retained history, and restore notes. Historical records remain historical. These are illustrative locations, not links to files installed by this worksheet. A separate project index points to `learning-loop-v1`. That record remains the sole selector of current task instructions. `action-list-rule-rationale-v1` links the instructions to their evidence and explains them without issuing a competing instruction. **Promotion candidate rejected:** “Never infer anything from meeting notes.” It is broader than the supported problem and would prohibit useful interpretation or clearly labeled proposals. **Approved principle:** “When turning supplied notes into commitments, preserve the distinction between what was agreed, what was suggested, and what remains unknown.” Scope: Fieldwork action-list practice design and review. Support: selected owner and deadline comparisons linked through the project rationale. Limit: synthetic design work, no observed learner benefit or universal detection guarantee. Current task instructions must still be retrieved through `learning-loop-v1`. **Promotion check:** Maya reopens the saved explanatory principle, checks its wording and scope, and follows its links. She confirms that it points to the existing instruction route rather than supplying a new version selector. **Retrieval request:** Find the applicable rule for an agreed item with no owner, then its rationale. The expected response keeps the action visible and marks assignment as not established; it does not invent an owner or suppress the action. **Unanswerable request:** Identify the person who should take that action. The source does not establish an assignment. The result must expose the gap. **Misleading route:** Search returns the rejected “every action must have an owner” candidate. Its heading identifies its rejected status and points toward the current instruction route. **Update rule:** Review each proposal against the version current at approval, save the approved new version, reopen it, update only the current selector in `learning-loop-v1`, and label the predecessor superseded. Update related rationale only when the reason changes. Do not start dependent work halfway through the change. **Restore failure:** The selected snapshot opens, but a rationale link reaches into the original workspace. It cannot support recovery independently of that original location. **Repair:** Include the authorized synthetic dependency, repair the relative link, and repeat from a new separate restore copy. Open the pointer, instructions, rationale, and evidence from that copy. **Behavior check:** Use a fresh synthetic input containing the imprecise timing “soon.” Check whether the result preserves the uncertainty rather than inventing a date. Record this separately from successful file opening. **Limits:** A same-device rehearsal does not establish protection against device loss, complete backup coverage, deletion from unknown copies, or equivalent behavior with another model. A matching manifest establishes only consistency of listed file bytes against that manifest.

title: Acceptance criteria
text: Each role has an actual location and a named approval boundary. The current instruction has one unambiguous selection route; explanatory notes and archived versions cannot silently override it. The promoted record is supported, scoped, approved, and reopened after saving. Retrieval finds the governing instruction and evidence, and preserves an unresolved answer when appropriate. A separately restored working set opens, retains its links and status labels, and supports a fresh task check. Availability, correct retrieval, and correct application are recorded as different results. Remaining dependencies and recovery limitations are visible.

title: Common failures and repair
text: Failure Repair A polished candidate is treated as current Keep it proposed; require a specific verdict; use the designated current pointer. Multiple overview files copy changing instructions Replace duplicated authority with descriptive links to the existing selector. Newer proposal overwrites a separately approved change Compare the proposal's starting version with the current version; apply only the intended reviewed change. Restored file refers to “the example above” or the original workspace Include the authorized dependency and a portable location; repeat from the copied package. File integrity passes but obsolete guidance is applied Inspect version authority, scope, and current decisions; rerun the semantic task. The architecture creates more maintenance than useful retrieval Reduce the working set and remove duplicate roles; preserve the charter and meaningful evidence. Keep this worksheet with the project. It records an exercised arrangement, not a claim that memory software or autonomous supervision has been implemented.
